techniques.name: Permutation Importance
techniques.description: Permutation Importance measures how much a trained model relies on each input feature. For each feature, the values in a dataset are shuffled at random, which breaks the link between that feature and the outcome, and the model is scored again. The fall in score, for example in accuracy, is the feature's importance: a large fall means the model depends on the feature, and little or no fall means it does not. Repeating the shuffle several times shows how much the result varies. The method works with any model, but it shows what the model uses, not what causes the outcome in the world.

example_use_cases.description: Assessing which patient characteristics (e.g., age, blood pressure, cholesterol) matter most to a medical diagnosis model by shuffling each one in turn on held-out patients and recording the drop in performance, so a clinician can judge whether the model relies on clinically relevant factors.

A bank's model-risk team shuffles each input to a card-fraud model in turn on held-out transactions, to check the model leans on transaction behaviour and not on a field that leaks the answer, such as a case-handling code recorded after fraud was confirmed.

A flood-forecasting team shuffles each rainfall, river-level and soil-moisture input of a model trained on historic data, to check that forecasts depend on the physical drivers hydrologists expect and not on a calendar variable.

limitations.description: When features are strongly correlated, shuffling one leaves the model able to rely on its correlated partner, so both can show low importance even though the model uses them. Shuffling also creates feature combinations that do not occur in real data, which can distort the scores.

Computationally expensive for large datasets or complex models. The model is scored once per feature per shuffle, so cost grows with the number of features, the number of repeats and the size of the evaluation data. No retraining is needed.

The score for a feature includes the effect of its interactions with other features and cannot separate them from its own effect. If two features interact, shuffling either one lowers the score, so importances need not add up to the model's total performance.
The ranking can change with the scoring metric, particularly for imbalanced classification, where accuracy and F1-score can give different pictures of which features matter.

Scores computed on training data can reflect overfitting: a feature the model has memorised can look important even though it does not help on new data. Use held-out data, and repeat the shuffle to see how much the scores vary.

resources.title: Random Forests
resources.abstract: Random forests are a combination of tree predictors such that each tree depends on the values of a random vector sampled independently and with the same distribution for all trees in the forest. The generalization error for forests converges a.s. to a limit as the number of trees in the forest becomes large. The generalization error of a forest of tree classifiers depends on the strength of the individual trees in the forest and the correlation between them. Using a random selection of features to split each node yields error rates that compare favorably to Adaboost (Y. Freund & R. Schapire, Machine Learning: Proceedings of the Thirteenth International conference, ***, 148–156), but are more robust with respect to noise. Internal estimates monitor error, strength, and correlation and these are used to show the response to increasing the number of features used in the splitting. Internal estimates are also used to measure variable importance. These ideas are also applicable to regression.

resources.title: All Models are Wrong, but Many are Useful: Learning a Variable's Importance by Studying an Entire Class of Prediction Models Simultaneously
resources.abstract: Variable importance (VI) tools describe how much covariates contribute to a prediction model's accuracy. However, important variables for one well-performing model (for example, a linear model $f(\mathbf{x})=\mathbf{x}^{T}β$ with a fixed coefficient vector $β$) may be unimportant for another model. In this paper, we propose model class reliance (MCR) as the range of VI values across all well-performing model in a prespecified class. Thus, MCR gives a more comprehensive description of importance by accounting for the fact that many prediction models, possibly of different parametric forms, may fit the data well. In the process of deriving MCR, we show several informative results for permutation-based VI estimates, based on the VI measures used in Random Forests. Specifically, we derive connections between permutation importance estimates for a single prediction model, U-statistics, conditional variable importance, conditional causal effects, and linear model coefficients. We then give probabilistic bounds for MCR, using a novel, generalizable technique. We apply MCR to a public data set of Broward County criminal records to study the reliance of recidivism prediction models on sex and race. In this application, MCR can be used to help inform VI for unknown, proprietary models.

resources.title: RANDOM FORESTS FOR CLASSIFICATION IN ECOLOGY
resources.abstract: Classification procedures are some of the most widely used statistical methods in ecology. Random forests (RF) is a new and powerful statistical classifier that is well established in other disciplines but is relatively unknown in ecology. Advantages of RF compared to other statistical classifiers include (1) very high classification accuracy; (2) a novel method of determining variable importance; (3) ability to model complex interactions among predictor variables; (4) flexibility to perform several types of statistical data analysis, including regression, classification, survival analysis, and unsupervised learning; and (5) an algorithm for imputing missing values. We compared the accuracies of RF and four other commonly used statistical classifiers using data on invasive plant species presence in Lava Beds National Monument, California, USA, rare lichen species presence in the Pacific Northwest, USA, and nest sites for cavity nesting birds in the Uinta Mountains, Utah, USA. We observed high classification accuracy in all applications as measured by cross-validation and, in the case of the lichen data, by independent test data, when comparing RF to other common classification methods. We also observed that the variables that RF identified as most important for classifying invasive plant species coincided with expectations based on the literature.

techniques.name: Permutation Tests
techniques.description: A permutation test asks how likely an observed result would be if there were no real relationship in the data. The tester shuffles the data many times in a way that breaks the relationship under test, recalculates the metric each time, and takes the p-value as the share of shuffled results at least as extreme as the real one. Shuffling the outcome labels and retraining tests whether a classifier's accuracy beats chance, and shuffling group membership tests whether a gap between groups in the rate of decisions, such as approvals, is larger than chance would produce. A restricted variant, Ojala and Garriga's second test, shuffles each feature's values separately within each class, which keeps every feature's own spread but breaks the relationships between features, so a classifier that makes significantly fewer errors on the real data than on the shuffled copies is using those relationships. The test needs no assumption about the shape of the data's distribution, but a small p-value does not show that an effect is large, important or causal.

example_use_cases.description: A hospital research group trains a classifier on 80 patients with thousands of gene-expression measurements. With so few cases, a good cross-validated accuracy could be luck, so it repeats the whole training and testing procedure on thousands of label-shuffled copies and reports the result only if it beats nearly all of them.

A council analytics team replacing a case-prioritisation model checks whether the new model's higher accuracy on the same test cases could be chance. It randomly swaps the two models' predictions case by case 10,000 times, recomputes the gap each time, and switches only if the real gap is larger than nearly all of the shuffled ones.

A bank's model-risk team sees a higher approval rate for one applicant group than another in a loan model's decisions. Before escalating, it shuffles group membership across applicants thousands of times and recomputes the gap, to test whether a gap this large could arise by chance. A significant gap prompts a fuller review but does not by itself show unlawful discrimination.

A cardiology team using a gradient-boosted model to flag high blood pressure expects height and weight to matter together, not only alone. It shuffles each feature within each outcome class 1,000 times and tests at the 5% level whether the model errs less on the real data, to decide if a simpler model treating features separately would do. A non-significant result means either the features are unrelated within classes or the model ignores the relationship.

limitations.description: Each permutation needs the metric recalculated, and a model may need retraining every time, so thousands of permutations of a large model can be expensive. Stricter thresholds need more permutations, because the smallest possible p-value is 1 divided by the number of permutations plus one, and repeated runs can disagree near the threshold.

Assumes exchangeability of observations under the null hypothesis, which may be violated in time series or hierarchical data structures, where simple shuffling gives p-values that are too small or too large.

A significant result shows that the data are unlikely under the stated null, such as 'features and labels are independent'. It does not show that the effect is large, important or causal, and shuffling cannot rule out a confounder or an artefact of how the data were collected.

Testing many features or groups at once produces some false positives by chance, so the p-values need correcting, for example with a false discovery rate procedure. Without that, a feature-by-feature test over many features will flag some that are only noise.

What is shuffled defines the question answered. Shuffling labels tests whether features and labels are related at all, while shuffling features within classes tests whether a classifier uses dependencies between features. The wrong scheme answers a different question from the one the assurance claim needs.

Permutation Tests for Studying Classifier Performance
resources.abstract: We explore the framework of permutation-based p-values for assessing the behavior of the classification error. In this paper we study two simple permutation tests. The first test estimates the null distribution by permuting the labels in the data; this has been used extensively in classification problems in computational biology. The second test produces permutations of the features within classes, inspired by restricted randomization techniques traditionally used in statistics. We study the properties of these tests and present an extensive empirical evaluation on real and synthetic data. Our analysis shows that studying the classification error via permutation tests is effective; in particular, the restricted permutation test clearly reveals whether the classifier exploits the interdependency between the features in the data.

resources.title: Nonparametric permutation tests for functional neuroimaging: A primer with examples
resources.abstract: Requiring only minimal assumptions for validity, nonparametric permutation testing provides a flexible and intuitive methodology for the statistical analysis of data from functional neuroimaging experiments, at some computational expense. Introduced into the functional neuroimaging literature by Holmes et al. ([ 1996 ]: J Cereb Blood Flow Metab 16:7–22), the permutation approach readily accounts for the multiple comparisons problem implicit in the standard voxel‐by‐voxel hypothesis testing framework. When the appropriate assumptions hold, the nonparametric permutation approach gives results similar to those obtained from a comparable Statistical Parametric Mapping approach using a general linear model with multiple comparisons corrections derived from random field theory. For analyses with low degrees of freedom, such as single subject PET/SPECT experiments or multi‐subject PET/SPECT or f MRI designs assessed for population effects, the nonparametric approach employing a locally pooled (smoothed) variance estimate can outperform the comparable Statistical Parametric Mapping approach. Thus, these nonparametric techniques can be used to verify the validity of less computationally expensive parametric approaches. Although the theory and relative advantages of permutation approaches have been discussed by various authors, there has been no accessible explication of the method, and no freely distributed software implementing it. Consequently, there have been few practical applications of the technique. This article, and the accompanying MATLAB software, attempts to address these issues. The standard nonparametric randomization and permutation testing ideas are developed at an accessible level, using practical examples from functional neuroimaging, and the extensions for multiple comparisons described. Three worked examples from PET and f MRI are presented, with discussion, and comparisons with standard parametric approaches made where appropriate. Practical considerations are given throughout, and relevant statistical concepts are expounded in appendices.

techniques.name: Adversarial Debiasing
techniques.description: Adversarial debiasing trains a model so that its predictions carry as little information as possible about a protected attribute, such as sex or race. Two neural networks are trained together, a predictor that learns the main task, such as estimating default risk, and an adversary that tries to guess each person's protected attribute from the predictor's output. The predictor is updated to stay accurate while making the adversary's guesses fail, which pushes its outputs towards equal rates of favourable outcomes across groups (demographic parity). If the adversary is also given the true label, the predictor is penalised only for information about the attribute beyond what the label carries, which targets equal error rates across groups (equalised odds). The method needs the protected attribute for every training example and a model trained by gradient descent.

example_use_cases.description: A technology company trains a CV-screening model with an adversary that tries to guess each applicant's gender from the model's shortlisting score, so that selection rates come out similar for men and women (demographic parity) instead of leaning on CV features that happen to correlate with gender.

A lender trains a default-risk model for loan approvals with an adversary that is given each applicant's score and true repayment outcome and tries to guess their age band, so that false-positive and false-negative rates are similar across age bands (equalised odds) while predictive accuracy is kept.

A hospital group trains a COVID-19 screening model on emergency-department data with an adversary that tries to guess patient ethnicity from the model's score and the true test result, so that error rates are similar across ethnic groups while screening performance stays clinically useful.

limitations.description: The adversary only sees what it is given, usually the predictor's score and, for equalised odds, the true label. The method therefore targets one output-level criterion and gives no assurance that hidden layers are free of protected-attribute information, or that a different criterion holds.
Needs the protected attribute for every training example, so it cannot be used where that attribute was never collected or may not be held.

Demographic parity and equalised odds generally cannot both be met, so one must be chosen before training. Equal error rates can also come from worsening one group's rates: in the original Adult income experiment, the false-positive rate for women rose from 0.025 to 0.065.

Training two networks against each other is unstable. The weight given to the adversary has to be tuned (adversary_loss_weight in AIF360), and a wrong setting can make training diverge or leave the result closer to a different criterion than the one intended.

The paper's guarantee that outputs meet the chosen criterion holds only if both networks converge and the adversary is strong enough. A weak adversary leaves bias in place, and the convexity assumptions behind the proof do not hold for typical neural networks, so fairness has to be checked on held-out data after training.

resources.title: On the Fairness ROAD: Robust Optimization for Adversarial Debiasing
resources.abstract: In the field of algorithmic fairness, significant attention has been put on group fairness criteria, such as Demographic Parity and Equalized Odds. Nevertheless, these objectives, measured as global averages, have raised concerns about persistent local disparities between sensitive groups. In this work, we address the problem of local fairness, which ensures that the predictor is unbiased not only in terms of expectations over the whole population, but also within any subregion of the feature space, unknown at training time. To enforce this objective, we introduce ROAD, a novel approach that leverages the Distributionally Robust Optimization (DRO) framework within a fair adversarial learning objective, where an adversary tries to infer the sensitive attribute from the predictions. Using an instance-level re-weighting strategy, ROAD is designed to prioritize inputs that are likely to be locally unfair, i.e. where the adversary faces the least difficulty in reconstructing the sensitive attribute. Numerical experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our method: it achieves Pareto dominance with respect to local fairness and accuracy for a given global fairness level across three standard datasets, and also enhances fairness generalization under distribution shift.

resources.title: Mitigating Unwanted Biases with Adversarial Learning
resources.abstract: Machine learning is a tool for building models that accurately represent input training data. When undesired biases concerning demographic groups are in the training data, well-trained models will reflect those biases. We present a framework for mitigating such biases by including a variable for the group of interest and simultaneously learning a predictor and an adversary. The input to the network X, here text or census data, produces a prediction Y, such as an analogy completion or income bracket, while the adversary tries to model a protected variable Z, here gender or zip code. The objective is to maximize the predictor's ability to predict Y while minimizing the adversary's ability to predict Z. Applied to analogy completion, this method results in accurate predictions that exhibit less evidence of stereotyping Z. When applied to a classification task using the UCI Adult (Census) Dataset, it results in a predictive model that does not lose much accuracy while achieving very close to equality of odds (Hardt, et al., 2016). The method is flexible and applicable to multiple definitions of fairness as well as a wide range of gradient-based learning models, including both regression and classification tasks.

resources.title: An adversarial training framework for mitigating algorithmic biases in clinical machine learning
resources.abstract: Machine learning is becoming increasingly prominent in healthcare. Although its benefits are clear, growing attention is being given to how these tools may exacerbate existing biases and disparities. In this study, we introduce an adversarial training framework that is capable of mitigating biases that may have been acquired through data collection. We demonstrate this proposed framework on the real-world task of rapidly predicting COVID-19, and focus on mitigating site-specific (hospital) and demographic (ethnicity) biases. Using the statistical definition of equalized odds, we show that adversarial training improves outcome fairness, while still achieving clinically-effective screening performances (negative predictive values >0.98). We compare our method to previous benchmarks, and perform prospective and external validation across four independent hospital cohorts. Our method can be generalized to any outcomes, models, and definitions of fairness.

Compared with the same model trained without the adversary, the model's gap on the chosen fairness criterion is smaller on held-out data, at a reported cost in accuracy.

techniques.name: Statistical Oversampling Methods
techniques.description: Statistical oversampling methods rebalance a training set by adding synthetic examples of an under-represented category instead of copying existing ones. The foundational method, SMOTE (Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique), takes a minority-class example, picks one of its nearest minority-class neighbours, and creates a new example at a random point on the line between the two in feature space. Variants differ in which examples seed the new points, such as Borderline-SMOTE (examples near the class boundary), ADASYN (examples with many neighbours from the other class) and SVMSMOTE (the support vectors of a support vector machine). Standard SMOTE balances the outcome labels and ignores group membership, so for fairness work the same generation is applied within each combination of protected group and label, making every combination equally large in the training data. Only the training data change, and plain SMOTE needs numeric features, with SMOTE-NC covering a mix of numeric and categorical ones.

example_use_cases.description: A bank's credit team finds that approved applicants from one ethnic group make up a small share of its loan training data. It adds synthetic approved applicants for that group with SMOTE until every group-and-outcome combination is the same size, then compares the approval-rate gap between groups, and the gap in approval of applicants who went on to repay, on held-out applications against a model trained on the original data.

A hospital analytics team building a readmission model finds that patients from one small ethnic group rarely appear among the readmitted cases. It applies Borderline-SMOTE within each group's readmitted cases, then reports recall for each group on held-out patients, with and without oversampling, to its clinical safety committee before deployment.

A university's student-support team builds a dropout-risk model from past cohorts in which students from low-income areas who left are few. It uses ADASYN to add synthetic examples for that combination, then checks on held-out cohorts that the model flags those students at a rate no further below the rate for other students than the model trained on the original data.

limitations.description: Plain SMOTE and its variants balance the outcome labels, not the groups, and can widen group gaps. In one study (logistic regression on the Adult income data), SMOTE raised the statistical parity difference between sexes from 0.21 to 0.33 (Chakraborty et al., 2021). Balancing protected-group-and-label combinations is needed for fairness, and the gaps must be measured on held-out data.

Synthetic points are interpolated from the few real examples already present, so they add no new information about a small group and do not repair why it is under-represented, such as how the data were collected. Counts on the oversampled set look larger than the real evidence behind them.

Interpolation assumes the space between two minority examples also belongs to the minority class. Where examples are scattered, overlap the majority class or include outliers, new points land in the wrong region and add label noise. ADASYN, which favours hard cases, can concentrate on outliers.

In high-dimensional data SMOTE mostly fails to correct the lean towards the majority class and is less effective than random undersampling. It lowers variability and makes synthetic points correlated, and with k-nearest-neighbour classifiers and no feature selection it tips predictions towards the minority class (Blagus and Lusa, 2013).

Oversampling before splitting the data, or before cross-validation, leaks information into the test set and inflates results. Resampling must touch only the training part, for example inside an imbalanced-learn Pipeline, and tests should use the natural class mix.

resources.title: SMOTE: Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique
resources.abstract: An approach to the construction of classifiers from    imbalanced datasets is described. A dataset is imbalanced if the    classification categories are not approximately equally    represented. Often real-world data sets are predominately composed of    ``normal'' examples with only a small percentage of ``abnormal'' or    ``interesting'' examples. It is also the case that the cost of    misclassifying an abnormal (interesting) example as a normal example    is often much higher than the cost of the reverse    error. Under-sampling of the majority (normal) class has been proposed    as a good means of increasing the sensitivity of a classifier to the    minority class. This paper shows that a combination of our method of    over-sampling the minority (abnormal) class and under-sampling the    majority (normal) class can achieve better classifier performance (in    ROC space) than only under-sampling the majority class.  This paper    also shows that a combination of our method of over-sampling the    minority class and under-sampling the majority class can achieve    better classifier performance (in ROC space) than varying the loss    ratios in Ripper or class priors in Naive Bayes. Our method of    over-sampling the minority class involves creating synthetic minority    class examples.  Experiments are performed using C4.5, Ripper and a    Naive Bayes classifier. The method is evaluated using the area under    the Receiver Operating Characteristic curve (AUC) and the ROC convex    hull strategy.

resources.title: ADASYN: Adaptive synthetic sampling approach for imbalanced learning
resources.abstract: This paper presents a novel adaptive synthetic (ADASYN) sampling approach for learning from imbalanced data sets. The essential idea of ADASYN is to use a weighted distribution for different minority class examples according to their level of difficulty in learning, where more synthetic data is generated for minority class examples that are harder to learn compared to those minority examples that are easier to learn. As a result, the ADASYN approach improves learning with respect to the data distributions in two ways: (1) reducing the bias introduced by the class imbalance, and (2) adaptively shifting the classification decision boundary toward the difficult examples. Simulation analyses on several machine learning data sets show the effectiveness of this method across five evaluation metrics.

SMOTE for high-dimensional class-imbalanced data
resources.abstract: BACKGROUND: Classification using class-imbalanced data is biased in favor of the majority class. The bias is even larger for high-dimensional data, where the number of variables greatly exceeds the number of samples. The problem can be attenuated by undersampling or oversampling, which produce class-balanced data. Generally undersampling is helpful, while random oversampling is not. Synthetic Minority Oversampling TEchnique (SMOTE) is a very popular oversampling method that was proposed to improve random oversampling but its behavior on high-dimensional data has not been thoroughly investigated. In this paper we investigate the properties of SMOTE from a theoretical and empirical point of view, using simulated and real high-dimensional data. RESULTS: While in most cases SMOTE seems beneficial with low-dimensional data, it does not attenuate the bias towards the classification in the majority class for most classifiers when data are high-dimensional, and it is less effective than random undersampling. SMOTE is beneficial for k-NN classifiers for high-dimensional data if the number of variables is reduced performing some type of variable selection; we explain why, otherwise, the k-NN classification is biased towards the minority class. Furthermore, we show that on high-dimensional data SMOTE does not change the class-specific mean values while it decreases the data variability and it introduces correlation between samples. We explain how our findings impact the class-prediction for high-dimensional data. CONCLUSIONS: In practice, in the high-dimensional setting only k-NN classifiers based on the Euclidean distance seem to benefit substantially from the use of SMOTE, provided that variable selection is performed before using SMOTE; the benefit is larger if more neighbors are used. SMOTE for k-NN without variable selection should not be used, because it strongly biases the classification towards the minority class.

resources.title: A Comparison of Undersampling, Oversampling, and SMOTE Methods for Dealing with Imbalanced Classification in Educational Data Mining
resources.abstract: Educational data mining is capable of producing useful data-driven applications (e.g., early warning systems in schools or the prediction of students’ academic achievement) based on predictive models. However, the class imbalance problem in educational datasets could hamper the accuracy of predictive models as many of these models are designed on the assumption that the predicted class is balanced. Although previous studies proposed several methods to deal with the imbalanced class problem, most of them focused on the technical details of how to improve each technique, while only a few focused on the application aspect, especially for the application of data with different imbalance ratios. In this study, we compared several sampling techniques to handle the different ratios of the class imbalance problem (i.e., moderately or extremely imbalanced classifications) using the High School Longitudinal Study of 2009 dataset. For our comparison, we used random oversampling (ROS), random undersampling (RUS), and the combination of the synthetic minority oversampling technique for nominal and continuous (SMOTE-NC) and RUS as a hybrid resampling technique. We used the Random Forest as our classification algorithm to evaluate the results of each sampling technique. Our results show that random oversampling for moderately imbalanced data and hybrid resampling for extremely imbalanced data seem to work best. The implications for educational data mining applications and suggestions for future research are discussed.

techniques.name: Quantile Regression
techniques.description: Quantile regression predicts chosen percentiles of an outcome, such as the 10th, 50th and 90th, rather than only its average. In the classical method a separate model is fitted for each percentile, using a loss that penalises under-prediction and over-prediction unequally. For example, instead of predicting an average house price of £300,000, it can predict that a house of a given size and location has a 10% chance of selling below £250,000 and a 90% chance of selling below £380,000. Comparing the fitted percentiles shows how features affect different parts of the outcome, such as size mattering more for expensive homes than for cheap ones. A low and a high percentile together give a prediction interval (a range expected to contain a new outcome) without assuming the errors are normally distributed, though how often the interval actually contains new outcomes must be checked on held-out data.

example_use_cases.description: Predicting patient recovery times after surgery by fitting the 10th, 50th and 90th percentiles, so clinicians can say 'most patients recover within 2 to 4 weeks, but one in ten takes longer than 8' when planning follow-up care and bed use.

A grid operator extends its wind power forecast with 10th and 90th percentile forecasts, fitted on past forecast errors and weather conditions, and sizes reserve capacity to the 90th percentile of the next-day shortfall rather than to an average error.

A flood-forecasting agency fits high percentiles of river level on rainfall and soil moisture, giving an upper bound that does not assume symmetric errors, and uses it to decide when to issue warnings for extreme events.

limitations.description: Cost grows with the number of quantile levels fitted when, as in the classical method, each level is a separate optimisation, which adds up on large datasets or with complex models.

May produce crossing quantiles without proper constraints, where predicted 90th percentile values are lower than 50th percentile values, creating logically inconsistent and unusable prediction intervals.

Extreme quantiles (for example the 5th or 95th) rest on few observations and, with heavy-tailed outcomes, are noisy and unstable. With small datasets they cannot be estimated reliably, because too few points lie in the tails.

Gives no guarantee that an interval built from two quantiles contains the stated share of new outcomes. Coverage can fall short if the model form is wrong or the data shift, so check it on held-out data before relying on it.

In its classical form each conditional quantile is assumed to be linear in the features. If the true relationship is curved or has interactions, the fitted quantiles are biased, and flexible models that avoid this lose the readable coefficients.

resources.abstract: For operational planning it is important to provide information about the situation‐dependent uncertainty of a wind power forecast. Factors which influence the uncertainty of a wind power forecast include the predictability of the actual meteorological situation, the level of the predicted wind speed (due to the non‐linearity of the power curve) and the forecast horizon. With respect to the predictability of the actual meteorological situation a number of explanatory variables are considered, some inspired by the literature. The article contains an overview of related work within the field. An existing wind power forecasting system (Zephyr/WPPT) is considered and it is shown how analysis of the forecast error can be used to build a model of the quantiles of the forecast error. Only explanatory variables or indices which are predictable are considered, whereby the model obtained can be used for providing situation‐dependent information regarding the uncertainty. Finally, the article contains directions enabling the reader to replicate the methods and thereby extend other forecast systems with situation‐dependent information on uncertainty.

techniques.name: Cross-validation
techniques.description: Cross-validation estimates how well a model will perform on data it has not seen, and how much that estimate depends on the particular data used. The dataset is divided into k parts called folds, the model is trained on all but one fold and scored on the held-out fold, and this repeats until every fold has served as the held-out set once. The scores are averaged to give a performance estimate, and their spread gives a rough indication of how much the result depends on which data the model was trained on. Common variants are stratified cross-validation, where each fold keeps the overall class proportions, and leave-one-out, where each fold is a single example. A large gap between training scores and held-out scores points to overfitting, where a model has learned quirks of its training data that do not carry over to new data.

example_use_cases.description: A hospital data-science team has records for about 900 patients and is building a readmission-risk model. It runs 10-fold cross-validation with each patient's admissions kept in the same fold, then reports the mean and spread of held-out scores. A wide spread, or a large gap to the training score, tells the team the model is not yet stable enough to take to a prospective trial.

A bank's fraud team compares three candidate classifiers by running the same stratified 10-fold cross-validation on a year of labelled transactions, so every candidate is scored on identical folds and the rare fraud cases are spread evenly across them. They select the model with the best mean recall at a fixed false-alarm rate and drop any candidate whose fold-to-fold scores vary widely.

A materials-science group has only 120 labelled samples from costly experiments. Instead of trusting one train-test split, it repeats 5-fold cross-validation with different random splits and reports the spread of the accuracy estimate, which decides whether the model is reliable enough to guide the next round of experiments.

limitations.description: The number of folds trades cost against bias and variance. Each fold is another training run. Few folds (2 to 5) train on less data and tend to understate performance, whereas leave-one-out has little bias but unstable estimates and the highest cost. Ten folds is a common compromise, not a rule.

Assumes records are independent. If the same patient, customer or site appears in several records, a fold can be trained on records nearly identical to those it is tested on, and the score is optimistic. Folds must then be built by group, not drawn at random.

Ignores time order. Training on later records and testing on earlier ones lets future information leak into the estimate and flatters the model. For time-ordered data, use an evaluation that always tests on data later than the training data, such as rolling-origin evaluation.

Anything learned from the data must be fitted inside each training fold, including scaling, feature selection and hyperparameter tuning. Done once on the full dataset beforehand, it leaks test-fold information and inflates the scores. Tuning and reporting on the same folds is also optimistic, so nested cross-validation is needed for both.

A score from a small sample is imprecise, and the spread across folds understates the true uncertainty. In one neuroimaging study, error bars on a cross-validated score were roughly plus or minus 10% with 100 samples, so a small gain between two models can be noise.

resources.abstract: Predictive models ground many state‐of‐the‐art developments in statistical brain image analysis: decoding, MVPA, searchlight, or extraction of biomarkers. The principled approach to establish their validity and usefulness is cross‐validation, testing prediction on unseen data. Simple experiments show that sample sizes of many neuroimaging studies inherently lead to large error bars, eg Symbol for 100 samples. The standard error across folds strongly underestimates them. These large error bars compromise the reliability of conclusions drawn with predictive models, such as biomarkers or methods developments where, unlike with cognitive neuroimaging MVPA approaches, more samples cannot be acquired by repeating the experiment across many subjects. techniques.name: Area Under Precision-Recall Curve
techniques.description: Area Under Precision-Recall Curve (AUPRC) summarises how well a classifier finds the cases that matter when those cases are rare. Precision is the share of positive predictions that are correct, and recall is the share of actual positives that are found. Plotting one against the other at every classification threshold gives a curve, and AUPRC is the area under it, from 0 to 1. Neither precision nor recall uses true negatives, so a large majority class does not flatter the score as it can flatter accuracy and AUC-ROC. A model with no skill scores about the proportion of positives in the data, so the score is only meaningful next to that baseline.

example_use_cases.description: A payments team compares candidate fraud models on a held-out month of transactions in which about 1 in 500 is fraudulent. It ranks them by AUPRC against the 0.2% no-skill baseline, then reads the best model's curve to choose a threshold that keeps false alarms within what the investigation team can review.

A hospital evaluates a model that screens for a rare condition affecting about 1 in 200 patients. ROC AUC can look high even when most flagged patients are healthy, so the team reports AUPRC against the 0.5% baseline and reads the precision at the recall clinicians require, to decide whether the follow-up workload is manageable.

A manufacturer compares two defect-detection models for a production line where about 1 in 1,000 parts is faulty. It uses AUPRC on a labelled validation batch to choose between them, so that a model is not preferred simply for labelling nearly every good part correctly.

limitations.description: AUPRC depends on the share of positives in the data, so scores from datasets or groups with different proportions cannot be compared directly, and no universal pass mark can be set. Each score has to be read against its own no-skill baseline, which is about the positive proportion.

It treats one class as the positive class and ignores true negatives, so it says nothing about how reliably the model clears the majority class. That matters where certifying a case as negative or safe is as important as catching positives.

A single area averages over every threshold, including ones no deployment would use, and can hide poor precision at the recall the application needs. Choosing the operating point needs a look at that part of the curve and the cost of each kind of error.

The area can be computed in different ways. Trapezoidal linear interpolation between points gives an overly optimistic value, whereas step-wise average precision does not, so scores from different libraries or settings may not match.
Few positive test cases make precision-recall estimates unstable, so a high score from a small sample may not hold on a larger, representative evaluation set.

resources.title: The relationship between Precision-Recall and ROC curves
resources.abstract: Receiver Operator Characteristic (ROC) curves are commonly used to present results for binary decision problems in machine learning. However, when dealing with highly skewed datasets, Precision-Recall (PR) curves give a more informative picture of an algorithm's performance. We show that a deep connection exists between ROC space and PR space, such that a curve dominates in ROC space if and only if it dominates in PR space. A corollary is the notion of an achievable PR curve, which has properties much like the convex hull in ROC space; we show an efficient algorithm for computing this curve. Finally, we also note differences in the two types of curves are significant for algorithm design. For example, in PR space it is incorrect to linearly interpolate between points. Furthermore, algorithms that optimize the area under the ROC curve are not guaranteed to optimize the area under the PR curve.

techniques.name: Monotonicity Constraints
techniques.description: Monotonicity constraints require a model's prediction to move only one way as a chosen input rises, with the other inputs held fixed, so that, for example, predicted salary never falls as years of experience increase. The direction for each constrained feature is set from domain knowledge before training, and the learning algorithm or model structure then rules out any fit that breaks it, so the model cannot learn reversals that come from noise or sampling quirks in the data. Boosted-tree libraries apply the constraint when they choose splits and monotonic neural networks build it into their structure, while penalty-based methods only discourage violations. Because a penalty, a constraint set on the wrong column or a later processing step can still let a reversal through, testers then vary each constrained input across its range over many generated or real cases, with the other inputs fixed, and count any prediction that moves the wrong way. The evidence is that violation count, expected to be zero, together with a comparison of held-out accuracy with and without the constraint.

example_use_cases.description: A mortgage lender constrains its approval model so that higher income, longer employment and a higher credit score can only raise the approval score. Loan officers can then tell an applicant that improving any of these factors can only help the application, and the lender can state each factor's direction to its regulator.

A water utility's pipe-burst risk model is constrained so that risk rises with pipe age and operating pressure and falls with the quality of recent maintenance. Asset managers can then explain the ranked inspection list to the regulator through three directional rules, instead of an opaque score.

A hospital analytics team builds a tree-based model that predicts the cost of care for each patient and constrains the prediction never to fall as age or number of chronic conditions rises. Before release they sweep each constrained feature across its range for thousands of generated patient records, with the other features held fixed, and confirm that no prediction moves the wrong way. They also compare held-out accuracy with and without the constraints.

A utility's day-ahead demand forecast for office buildings is constrained so that predicted demand never falls as occupancy or floor area rises. The validation team writes this as an automated test that draws random building profiles, raises one constrained input at a time and fails the build if any forecast drops, so a retrained model that breaks the rule is caught before deployment.

limitations.description: Forces a one-way relationship even where the real one reverses, such as an inverted U between experience and performance. The model then fits that feature worse and cannot show the turning point, so held-out accuracy should be compared with and without the constraint.

Choosing which features to constrain, and in which direction, needs domain expertise. A wrong constraint builds a false belief into the model, and the check on the trained model will still pass, because it shows only that the constraint holds, not that it is right.

The rule covers one feature with the others held fixed, and says nothing about the size of the effect. A model can meet it by ignoring the feature, and when correlated inputs move together a person's overall score can still fall as one favourable input rises, so the constraint does not make the whole model easy to explain.

Support differs by model family. Tree-boosting libraries such as XGBoost accept constraints directly, while neural networks need a special architecture or a penalty term. With histogram-based tree methods, constraints can remove every candidate split and leave shallow trees that underfit.

A sweep or property-based test samples the input space. It can find a violation but cannot prove there is none, and a pass depends on how well the generated inputs cover realistic and rare combinations of features.

This research suggests the application of monotonicity constraints to the back propagation learning algorithm. When the training sample set is preprocessed by a linear classification function, neural network performance and efficiency can be improved in classification applications where the feature vector is related monotonically to the pattern vector. Since most classification problems in business possess monotonic properties, this technique is useful in those problems where any assumptions about the properties of the data are inappropriate.

resources.title: An informed monotone neural network for multi-stage chronic kidney disease prediction with integrated GFR estimation
resources.abstract: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is a progressive condition affecting over 850 million people worldwide, where timely detection and accurate staging are critical to reducing morbidity, mortality, and healthcare burden. Current machine learning approaches often treat CKD prediction as a binary task, neglecting the ordered nature of disease stages, and rarely incorporate physiological constraints or calibrated probability estimates essential for clinical decision support. We propose a multi-stage CKD prediction framework that integrates ordinal classification, probability calibration, and a serum creatinine-monotonicity constraint within a knowledge distillation paradigm. A calibrated CatBoost model serves as a teacher, transferring temperature-scaled class probabilities to an ordinal neural network student augmented with an auxiliary eGFR regression task. Evaluated on a cohort of 750 patients from Al-Ramadi Teaching Hospital, our approach achieved superior macro-F1 and reduced expected calibration error. This work demonstrates that combining ordinal learning, calibration, and physiological constraints yields models that are not only accurate but also aligned with clinical reasoning, offering a pathway toward safer and more trustworthy AI tools for CKD management. Limitations like circular reasoning and target leakage are also discussed.

techniques.name: Generalized Additive Models
techniques.description: A generalised additive model (GAM) builds its prediction by adding a baseline and one smooth curve for each input feature. It extends linear and logistic regression by letting each feature's effect bend, so the model can follow patterns such as risk that climbs steeply after a certain age. Each curve is learned from the data with a smoothing method, such as splines (flexible curves built from joined polynomial pieces). Plotting the curves shows how each feature moves the prediction across its range, so the model can be read directly without a separate explanation method. Because the curves are added together, the model does not capture the joint effect of two features unless a combined term is added by hand.

example_use_cases.description: A hospital builds its 30-day readmission model as a GAM so that its governance committee can audit it. The committee reviews one curve each for age, blood pressure and medication adherence, and queries any stretch where predicted risk falls as a known risk factor rises, since that can point to a data problem rather than a real effect.

A lender uses a GAM for credit scoring so that it can tell a declined applicant how income, credit history and debt-to-income ratio each moved their score. Each factor has its own curve, so the explanation comes straight from the model and needs no separate explanation tool.

An environmental agency models river nitrate levels with a GAM and plots the curve for rainfall. The curve shows the effect levelling off above a certain rainfall, which analysts report to catchment managers instead of a single regression coefficient.

limitations.description: Each feature acts separately, so the model cannot represent effects that depend on two features together, such as the impact of a dose varying with age. Product terms can be added by hand, but each must be thought of in advance and adds a surface that is harder to read than a curve.

The smoothness of each curve is a modelling choice. Cross-validation or penalised fitting selects it automatically, but too little smoothing gives wiggly curves that look like real effects and too much hides genuine bends, so each curve should be read with its confidence band.

When features are strongly related, such as income and age, a nonlinear form of collinearity called concurvity lets one curve absorb part of another's effect. The individual curves can then misstate how much each feature influences the prediction.

A model with dozens of smooth terms produces dozens of curves. Reading them all is slow, so reviewers tend to inspect only the largest effects, and the transparency benefit shrinks as the number of terms grows.
Terms add on the chosen link scale. In a logistic GAM they are contributions to log-odds, not independent additions to readmission probability or guaranteed causal feature effects.

Generalized Additive Models
resources.abstract: Likelihood-based regression models such as the normal linear regression model and the linear logistic model, assume a linear (or some other parametric) form for the covariates X1, X2, …, Xp. We introduce the class of generalized additive models which replaces the linear form Σ βjXj by a sum of smooth functions Σ sj(Xj). The sj(·)'s are unspecified functions that are estimated using a scatterplot smoother, in an iterative procedure we call the local scoring algorithm. The technique is applicable to any likelihood-based regression model: the class of generalized linear models contains many of these. In this class the linear predictor η = Σ βjXj is replaced by the additive predictor Σ sj(Xj); hence, the name generalized additive models. We illustrate the technique with binary response and survival data. In both cases, the method proves to be useful in uncovering nonlinear covariate effects. It has the advantage of being completely automatic, i.e., no "detective work" is needed on the part of the statistician. As a theoretical underpinning, the technique is viewed as an empirical method of maximizing the expected log likelihood, or equivalently, of minimizing the Kullback-Leibler distance to the true model.

resources.title: Fast Stable Restricted Maximum Likelihood and Marginal Likelihood Estimation of Semiparametric Generalized Linear Models
resources.abstract: Recent work by Reiss and Ogden provides a theoretical basis for sometimes preferring restricted maximum likelihood (REML) to generalized cross-validation (GCV) for smoothing parameter selection in semiparametric regression. However, existing REML or marginal likelihood (ML) based methods for semiparametric generalized linear models (GLMs) use iterative REML or ML estimation of the smoothing parameters of working linear approximations to the GLM. Such indirect schemes need not converge and fail to do so in a non-negligible proportion of practical analyses. By contrast, very reliable prediction error criteria smoothing parameter selection methods are available, based on direct optimization of GCV, or related criteria, for the GLM itself. Since such methods directly optimize properly defined functions of the smoothing parameters, they have much more reliable convergence properties. The paper develops the first such method for REML or ML estimation of smoothing parameters. A Laplace approximation is used to obtain an approximate REML or ML for any GLM, which is suitable for efficient direct optimization. This REML or ML criterion requires that Newton–Raphson iteration, rather than Fisher scoring, be used for GLM fitting, and a computationally stable approach to this is proposed. The REML or ML criterion itself is optimized by a Newton method, with the derivatives required obtained by a mixture of implicit differentiation and direct methods. The method will cope with numerical rank deficiency in the fitted model and in fact provides a slight improvement in numerical robustness on the earlier method of Wood for prediction error criteria based smoothness selection. Simulation results suggest that the new REML and ML methods offer some improvement in mean-square error performance relative to GCV or Akaike’s information criterion in most cases, without the small number of severe undersmoothing failures to which Akaike’s information criterion and GCV are prone. This is achieved at the same computational cost as GCV or Akaike’s information criterion. The new approach also eliminates the convergence failures of previous REML- or ML-based approaches for penalized GLMs and usually has lower computational cost than these alternatives. Example applications are presented in adaptive smoothing, scalar on function regression and generalized additive model selection.

Intelligible Models for HealthCare
resources.abstract: In machine learning often a tradeoff must be made between accuracy and intelligibility. More accurate models such as boosted trees, random forests, and neural nets usually are not intelligible, but more intelligible models such as logistic regression, naive-Bayes, and single decision trees often have significantly worse accuracy. This tradeoff sometimes limits the accuracy of models that can be applied in mission-critical applications such as healthcare where being able to understand, validate, edit, and trust a learned model is important. We present two case studies where high-performance generalized additive models with pairwise interactions (GA2Ms) are applied to real healthcare problems yielding intelligible models with state-of-the-art accuracy. In the pneumonia risk prediction case study, the intelligible model uncovers surprising patterns in the data that previously had prevented complex learned models from being fielded in this domain, but because it is intelligible and modular allows these patterns to be recognized and removed. In the 30-day hospital readmission case study, we show that the same methods scale to large datasets containing hundreds of thousands of patients and thousands of attributes while remaining intelligible and providing accuracy comparable to the best (unintelligible) machine learning methods.

Each nonlinear effect the model reports departs from a straight line by more than the width of its confidence band, so the bend is not an artefact of over-flexible smoothing.

techniques.name: Concept Activation Vectors
techniques.description: A concept activation vector (CAV) is a direction inside a neural network that stands for a human idea such as 'stripes'. The analyst supplies example inputs showing the concept and random counter-examples, and trains a simple linear classifier to separate the network's activations (the values a chosen layer produces) for the two sets. The CAV is the direction at right angles to that classifier's dividing boundary, pointing towards the concept examples. Testing with CAVs (TCAV) then reports, for one output class, the share of its inputs whose class score would rise if the activations moved in the concept's direction, and repeating this with many random counter-example sets and applying a significance test guards against a meaningless direction. Concept sets built from examples of a protected characteristic, such as gender or ethnicity, turn the test into a check of whether a class is sensitive to that characteristic, as the original paper demonstrates.

example_use_cases.description: Auditing a medical imaging model to check whether its chest X-ray classifications are sensitive to diagnostic concepts (like 'tumour characteristics') or to irrelevant ones (like 'scanner type' or 'patient positioning'), so the clinical team can judge whether the model relies on medically relevant information.

A team auditing an image classifier used for content tagging builds concept sets from photographs of people of different ethnicities and genders, with random photographs as the comparison, and tests each output class for significant sensitivity to those concepts, as the original paper did. Classes with significant sensitivity to an ethnicity or gender concept are listed for retraining with balanced data; a low score is not taken as clearance.

A developer of a driver-assistance system documents, for a type-approval authority, how its traffic-sign classifier responds to visual concepts. The report gives significance-tested TCAV scores for the 'stop sign' class against concepts such as graffiti, snow cover and low sun glare, so the authority can see what the classifier's predictions are sensitive to.

limitations.description: Requires clearly defined concept examples and non-concept examples, which can be hard to obtain for abstract or subjective concepts. If the examples differ from the random counter-examples in other ways, such as image source or lighting, the CAV mixes those differences in with the concept.

Assumes the concept is represented as a direction that a linear classifier can pick out at the chosen layer. If the concept is not linearly separable there, the CAV is unreliable, so check that the classifier separates the two sets well before reading any scores.

Results depend heavily on which layer is examined, because layers capture different levels of abstraction. A concept can be invisible at one layer and strong at another, so a single-layer result should not be generalised.

The significance test trains hundreds of classifiers per concept and layer (the paper uses about 500), so cost multiplies with the number of concepts and layers tested. FastCAV, a 2025 preprint, reports speed-ups of up to 63.6 times.

Scores are class-level and describe sensitivity, not cause. A TCAV score is the share of a class's inputs whose score rises along the concept direction, so it does not explain an individual decision, and a high score does not show that the concept causes the prediction.

resources.title: FastCAV: Efficient Computation of Concept Activation Vectors for Explaining Deep Neural Networks
resources.abstract: Concepts such as objects, patterns, and shapes are how humans understand the world. Building on this intuition, concept-based explainability methods aim to study representations learned by deep neural networks in relation to human-understandable concepts. Here, Concept Activation Vectors (CAVs) are an important tool and can identify whether a model learned a concept or not. However, the computational cost and time requirements of existing CAV computation pose a significant challenge, particularly in large-scale, high-dimensional architectures. To address this limitation, we introduce FastCAV, a novel approach that accelerates the extraction of CAVs by up to 63.6x (on average 46.4x). We provide a theoretical foundation for our approach and give concrete assumptions under which it is equivalent to established SVM-based methods. Our empirical results demonstrate that CAVs calculated with FastCAV maintain similar performance while being more efficient and stable. In downstream applications, i.e., concept-based explanation methods, we show that FastCAV can act as a replacement leading to equivalent insights. Hence, our approach enables previously infeasible investigations of deep models, which we demonstrate by tracking the evolution of concepts during model training.

resources.title: Interpretability Beyond Feature Attribution: Quantitative Testing with Concept Activation Vectors (TCAV)
resources.abstract: The interpretation of deep learning models is a challenge due to their size, complexity, and often opaque internal state. In addition, many systems, such as image classifiers, operate on low-level features rather than high-level concepts. To address these challenges, we introduce Concept Activation Vectors (CAVs), which provide an interpretation of a neural net’s internal state in terms of human-friendly concepts. The key idea is to view the high-dimensional internal state of a neural net as an aid, not an obstacle. We show how to use CAVs as part of a technique, Testing with CAVs (TCAV), that uses directional derivatives to quantify the degree to which a user-defined concept is important to a classification result–for example, how sensitive a prediction of “zebra” is to the presence of stripes. Using the domain of image classification as a testing ground, we describe how CAVs may be used to explore hypotheses and generate insights for a standard image classification network as well as a medical application.

resources.title: Global and Local Interpretability for Cardiac MRI Classification
resources.abstract: Deep learning methods for classifying medical images have demonstrated impressive accuracy in a wide range of tasks but often these models are hard to interpret, limiting their applicability in clinical practice. In this work we introduce a convolutional neural network model for identifying disease in temporal sequences of cardiac MR segmentations which is interpretable in terms of clinically familiar measurements. The model is based around a variational autoencoder, reducing the input into a low-dimensional latent space in which classification occurs. We then use the recently developed `concept activation vector' technique to associate concepts which are diagnostically meaningful (eg. clinical biomarkers such as `low left-ventricular ejection fraction') to certain vectors in the latent space. These concepts are then qualitatively inspected by observing the change in the image domain resulting from interpolations in the latent space in the direction of these vectors. As a result, when the model classifies images it is also capable of providing naturally interpretable concepts relevant to that classification and demonstrating the meaning of those concepts in the image domain. Our approach is demonstrated on the UK Biobank cardiac MRI dataset where we detect the presence of coronary artery disease.

resources.title: Concept attribution: Explaining CNN decisions to physicians
resources.abstract: Deep learning explainability is often reached by gradient-based approaches that attribute the network output to perturbations of the input pixels. However, the relevance of input pixels may be difficult to relate to relevant image features in some applications, e.g. diagnostic measures in medical imaging. The framework described in this paper shifts the attribution focus from pixel values to user-defined concepts. By checking if certain diagnostic measures are present in the learned representations, experts can explain and entrust the network output. Being post-hoc, our method does not alter the network training and can be easily plugged into the latest state-of-the-art convolutional networks. This paper presents the main components of the framework for attribution to concepts, in addition to the introduction of a spatial pooling operation on top of the feature maps to obtain a solid interpretability analysis. Furthermore, regularized regression is analyzed as a solution to the regression overfitting in high-dimensionality latent spaces. The versatility of the proposed approach is shown by experiments on two medical applications, namely histopathology and retinopathy, and on one non-medical task, the task of handwritten digit classification. The obtained explanations are in line with clinicians' guidelines and complementary to widely used visualization tools such as saliency maps.

techniques.name: Reweighing
techniques.description: Reweighing is a fairness method, presented by Kamiran and Calders (2012), that adjusts the training data before any model is trained so that a protected attribute, such as sex or ethnicity, has no statistical link to the outcome label. It does this by giving each training example a weight, leaving every feature value and label unchanged. Each combination of group and label (for example, women who were hired) gets a weight equal to the number of examples it would hold if group and label were unrelated, divided by the number it actually holds. Combinations rarer than that expectation, such as positive outcomes in a disadvantaged group, are weighted up and over-represented ones are weighted down, so every group has the same rate of positive labels in the weighted data. A model is then trained on the original data with these weights, so the learning algorithm must accept example weights.

example_use_cases.description: A bank's model team finds that in the historical loan decisions used as training labels, applicants from one ethnic group were approved far less often than others. Before retraining its approval model it computes reweighing weights, so that approved applicants from that group count for more and refused ones for less, trains with them as sample weights, and compares the approval-rate gap and accuracy on held-out data against the unweighted model.

A health insurer's analytics team building a model to target postpartum depression outreach from Medicaid claims compares reweighing by race with simply removing race from the inputs. It reports each option's disparate impact ratio (the ratio of positive-prediction rates between groups) and predictive performance to its clinical governance group before choosing one.

A recruitment platform training a shortlisting model on past hiring outcomes, in which women were hired into senior engineering roles less often than men, applies reweighing by sex before training so that the weighted history shows equal hiring rates, then checks shortlisting rates by sex on a held-out set of applications.

limitations.description: Its target is fixed: equal rates of positive labels across groups in the weighted training data (statistical parity). It does not aim at equal error rates such as equal opportunity, and the weights are computed once, before training, so they cannot respond to where the trained model actually errs. An adaptive variant (Krasanakis et al., 2018) re-estimates weights during training for error-rate criteria, but it has no maintained implementation.

It removes all association between group and label, including any part a legitimate factor explains. Kamiran and Calders give the example of car insurance, where more accidents among men may justify different outcomes by sex; reweighing erases that difference too, so it over-corrects wherever some gap between groups is warranted.

The learning algorithm must accept example weights; where it cannot, the data have to be resampled instead, which is a different method. Only the training data are balanced, so the trained model's predictions are not guaranteed to be: outcome rates by group must be measured on held-out data after training rather than assumed.

When a group-label combination is rare its weight is large (a combination with a tenth of its expected count gets a weight of ten), so a handful of examples can dominate training. This raises variance and amplifies any labelling errors in exactly the group the method is meant to protect, and it bites hardest with small or intersectional groups.
An absent group-label combination cannot be created by weighting existing records. Zero observed counts require explicit handling rather than applying the ratio unchanged.

resources.title: Comparison of Methods to Reduce Bias From Clinical Prediction Models of Postpartum Depression
resources.abstract: Importance: The lack of standards in methods to reduce bias for clinical algorithms presents various challenges in providing reliable predictions and in addressing health disparities. Objective: To evaluate approaches for reducing bias in machine learning models using a real-world clinical scenario. Design, Setting, and Participants: Health data for this cohort study were obtained from the IBM MarketScan Medicaid Database. Eligibility criteria were as follows: (1) Female individuals aged 12 to 55 years with a live birth record identified by delivery-related codes from January 1, 2014, through December 31, 2018; (2) greater than 80% enrollment through pregnancy to 60 days post partum; and (3) evidence of coverage for depression screening and mental health services. Statistical analysis was performed in 2020. Exposures: Binarized race (Black individuals and White individuals). Main Outcomes and Measures: Machine learning models (logistic regression [LR], random forest, and extreme gradient boosting) were trained for 2 binary outcomes: postpartum depression (PPD) and postpartum mental health service utilization. Risk-adjusted generalized linear models were used for each outcome to assess potential disparity in the cohort associated with binarized race (Black or White). Methods for reducing bias, including reweighing, Prejudice Remover, and removing race from the models, were examined by analyzing changes in fairness metrics compared with the base models. Baseline characteristics of female individuals at the top-predicted risk decile were compared for systematic differences. Fairness metrics of disparate impact (DI, 1 indicates fairness) and equal opportunity difference (EOD, 0 indicates fairness). Results: Among 573 634 female individuals initially examined for this study, 314 903 were White (54.9%), 217 899 were Black (38.0%), and the mean (SD) age was 26.1 (5.5) years. The risk-adjusted odds ratio comparing White participants with Black participants was 2.06 (95% CI, 2.02-2.10) for clinically recognized PPD and 1.37 (95% CI, 1.33-1.40) for postpartum mental health service utilization. Taking the LR model for PPD prediction as an example, reweighing reduced bias as measured by improved DI and EOD metrics from 0.31 and -0.19 to 0.79 and 0.02, respectively. Removing race from the models had inferior performance for reducing bias compared with the other methods (PPD: DI = 0.61; EOD = -0.05; mental health service utilization: DI = 0.63; EOD = -0.04). Conclusions and Relevance: Clinical prediction models trained on potentially biased data may produce unfair outcomes on the basis of the chosen metrics. This study's results suggest that the performance varied depending on the model, outcome label, and method for reducing bias. This approach toward evaluating algorithmic bias can be used as an example for the growing number of researchers who wish to examine and address bias in their data and models.

resources.title: Bias Discovery in Machine Learning Models for Mental Health
resources.abstract: Fairness and bias are crucial concepts in artificial intelligence, yet they are relatively ignored in machine learning applications in clinical psychiatry. We computed fairness metrics and present bias mitigation strategies using a model trained on clinical mental health data. We collected structured data related to the admission, diagnosis, and treatment of patients in the psychiatry department of the University Medical Center Utrecht. We trained a machine learning model to predict future administrations of benzodiazepines on the basis of past data. We found that gender plays an unexpected role in the predictions—this constitutes bias. Using the AI Fairness 360 package, we implemented reweighing and discrimination-aware regularization as bias mitigation strategies, and we explored their implications for model performance. This is the first application of bias exploration and mitigation in a machine learning model trained on real clinical psychiatry data.

techniques.name: Fairness GAN
techniques.description: Fairness GAN is a pre-processing method that generates a synthetic training dataset in which decisions no longer track a protected attribute such as gender or skin tone. A generative adversarial network (GAN) is a pair of networks trained against each other, one producing fake examples and one trying to tell them from real ones. Here the generator is conditioned on the protected attribute and produces both an example and its decision label, such as hired or rejected (images in the original work, table rows in Xu et al.'s separate FairGAN). An extra network tries to predict the protected attribute from the generated output, and the generator is rewarded for defeating it, so favourable decisions become more similar across groups. The user can aim for demographic parity, meaning equal rates of favourable decisions, or for equality of opportunity, which applies the constraint only to favourable decisions.

example_use_cases.description: A recruitment technology team holds interview-video stills labelled with past shortlisting decisions that favoured one gender. It trains a Fairness GAN to generate a synthetic image set whose shortlisting labels are similar for women and men, trains the screening model on that set, and compares shortlisting rates by gender on held-out real images before deployment.

A lender's data science team has ten years of loan decisions in which women were approved less often than men on similar incomes. It trains a tabular FairGAN-style generator to produce a synthetic dataset, confirms that the gap in approval rates in the synthetic data is close to zero, and trains its scoring model on that data, testing accuracy and approval rates on real held-out applications.

limitations.description: GAN training is unstable and the fairness loss adds a further pull on the generator. The original authors used spectral normalisation, softened outcome values and added noise to keep training stable, and results still varied across datasets. Expect tuning effort and repeated runs.

Fairness and accuracy trade off, and the gain is uneven. In the original experiments a classifier trained on debiased CelebA data went from about 20 to about 29 per cent error. Demographic parity improved on three of four datasets but not on Quick, Draw!, and the demographic-parity version made equality of opportunity worse on the soccer data.

It needs a lot of data. The authors had only 1,501 labelled soccer images, so they borrowed more than 200,000 unlabelled CelebA faces to help the generator, which is possible only when a large related set exists.

The original method covers a narrow setting: image inputs, one binary protected attribute and a binary outcome, with demographic parity or equality of opportunity but not equalised odds. Continuous protected attributes and non-image data are left as future work, and tabular versions such as FairGAN are separate methods with their own evidence.

Fairness is judged by training a classifier on the synthetic data and testing it on real data, and image quality is judged mainly by inspecting average faces. The authors report that debiasing visibly changes images in stereotyped ways, such as male faces taking on features coded as feminine, so the synthetic data need checking for distortions that the classifier test would miss.
