resources.abstract: In this paper, we introduce the Fairness GAN, an approach for generating a dataset that is plausibly similar to a given multimedia dataset, but is more fair with respect to protected attributes in allocative decision making. We propose a novel auxiliary classifier GAN that strives for demographic parity or equality of opportunity and show empirical results on several datasets, including the CelebFaces Attributes (CelebA) dataset, the Quick, Draw!\ dataset, and a dataset of soccer player images and the offenses they were called for. The proposed formulation is well-suited to absorbing unlabeled data; we leverage this to augment the soccer dataset with the much larger CelebA dataset. The methodology tends to improve demographic parity and equality of opportunity while generating plausible images.

resources.title: FairGAN: Fairness-aware Generative Adversarial Networks
resources.abstract: Fairness-aware learning is increasingly important in data mining. Discrimination prevention aims to prevent discrimination in the training data before it is used to conduct predictive analysis. In this paper, we focus on fair data generation that ensures the generated data is discrimination free. Inspired by generative adversarial networks (GAN), we present fairness-aware generative adversarial networks, called FairGAN, which are able to learn a generator producing fair data and also preserving good data utility. Compared with the naive fair data generation models, FairGAN further ensures the classifiers which are trained on generated data can achieve fair classification on real data. Experiments on a real dataset show the effectiveness of FairGAN.

resources.title: Bt-GAN: Generating Fair Synthetic Healthdata via Bias-transforming Generative Adversarial Networks
resources.abstract: Synthetic data generation offers a promising solution to enhance the usefulness of Electronic Healthcare Records (EHR) by generating realistic de-identified data. However, the existing literature primarily focuses on the quality of synthetic health data, neglecting the crucial aspect of fairness in downstream predictions. Consequently, models trained on synthetic EHR have faced criticism for producing biased outcomes in target tasks. These biases can arise from either spurious correlations between features or the failure of models to accurately represent sub-groups. To address these concerns, we present Bias-transforming Generative Adversarial Networks (Bt-GAN), a GAN-based synthetic data generator specifically designed for the healthcare domain. In order to tackle spurious correlations (i), we propose an information-constrained Data Generation Process (DGP) that enables the generator to learn a fair deterministic transformation based on a well-defined notion of algorithmic fairness. To overcome the challenge of capturing exact sub-group representations (ii), we incentivize the generator to preserve sub-group densities through score-based weighted sampling. This approach compels the generator to learn from underrepresented regions of the data manifold. To evaluate the effectiveness of our proposed method, we conduct extensive experiments using the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care (MIMIC-III) database. Our results demonstrate that Bt-GAN achieves state-of-the-art accuracy while significantly improving fairness and minimizing bias amplification. Furthermore, we perform an in-depth explainability analysis to provide additional evidence supporting the validity of our study. In conclusion, our research introduces a novel and professional approach to addressing the limitations of synthetic data generation in the healthcare domain. By incorporating fairness considerations and leveraging advanced techniques such as GANs, we pave the way for more reliable and unbiased predictions in healthcare applications.

resources.title: FairFinGAN: Fairness-Aware Synthetic Financial Data Generation
resources.abstract: Financial datasets often suffer from bias that can lead to unfair decision-making in automated systems. In this work, we propose FairFinGAN, a WGAN-based framework designed to generate synthetic financial data while mitigating bias with respect to the protected attribute. Our approach incorporates fairness constraints directly into the training process through a classifier, ensuring that the synthetic data is both fair and preserves utility for downstream predictive tasks. We evaluate our proposed model on five real-world financial datasets and compare it with existing GAN-based data generation methods. Experimental results show that our approach achieves superior fairness metrics without significant loss in data utility, demonstrating its potential as a tool for bias-aware data generation in financial applications.

techniques.name: Relabelling
techniques.description: Relabelling, also called data massaging, is a pre-processing method proposed by Kamiran and Calders. It changes some of the outcome labels in a training set so that a protected group and everyone else have the same rate of positive outcomes, such as being hired or approved. A ranking model first scores each example by how likely it is to be positive. The method then promotes the highest-scoring negative examples from the disadvantaged group to positive and demotes the lowest-scoring positive examples from the favoured group to negative, in equal numbers. Because the examples closest to the decision boundary change first and the numbers are equal, the overall share of positive labels stays the same and the number of changes is as small as it can be.

example_use_cases.description: A public-sector recruiter's ten years of shortlisting records show women shortlisted less often than men with comparable applications. Before training a screening model, the data team flips the labels of the rejected women a ranking model scores highest and the shortlisted men it scores lowest, in equal numbers, until shortlisting rates match and the overall shortlisting rate is unchanged.

A building society finds that past loan decisions approved applicants from one ethnic minority far less often than others with similar finances, and suspects the gap reflects past discretion rather than risk. It flips borderline decisions in both directions, keeping the overall approval rate fixed, and trains its scoring model on the corrected labels while keeping the original labels in a separate file.

limitations.description: It assumes the whole gap in positive rates between groups is discrimination. The number of labels changed is set to bring the gap to zero, even where part of the gap has a legitimate explanation, and the original authors note that such constraints are often too strong.

It rewrites the record of what happened. The flipped labels no longer match the real decisions or outcomes, so it suits labels that record biased past decisions and is dangerous where labels are measured facts, such as a confirmed diagnosis or a repayment. The authors call the approach intrusive.

Which records are flipped depends on a ranking model trained on the same biased data. A poor ranker flips the wrong people, and in the original experiments the discrimination and accuracy of the final classifier varied with the learner trained afterwards.

It handles one binary protected attribute and a binary outcome. Gender and ethnicity together, or a numeric attribute such as income, are not covered, so correcting one attribute can leave intersectional gaps.

Accuracy falls as discrimination falls, and the authors prove the trade-off cannot be avoided. Discrimination is removed from the training data, but a model trained on it can still show some on new data.

resources.title: Classifying without discriminating
resources.abstract: Classification models usually make predictions on the basis of training data. If the training data is biased towards certain groups or classes of objects, e.g., there is racial discrimination towards black people, the learned model will also show discriminatory behavior towards that particular community. This partial attitude of the learned model may lead to biased outcomes when labeling future unlabeled data objects. Often, however, impartial classification results are desired or even required by law for future data objects in spite of having biased training data. In this paper, we tackle this problem by introducing a new classification scheme for learning unbiased models on biased training data. Our method is based on massaging the dataset by making the least intrusive modifications which lead to an unbiased dataset. On this modified dataset we then learn a non-discriminating classifier. The proposed method has been implemented and experimental results on a credit approval dataset show promising results: in all experiments our method is able to reduce the prejudicial behavior for future classification significantly without loosing too much predictive accuracy.

The lending model trained on the corrected labels shows a smaller gap in approval rates between age groups on held-out data than a model trained on the original labels.

techniques.name: Preferential Sampling
techniques.description: Preferential Sampling is a pre-processing method, proposed by Kamiran and Calders, that rebalances a training set so that a protected group and everyone else have the same rate of positive outcomes, such as being hired or approved. A ranking model first scores every example by how likely it is to have a positive label. The method then compares the size of each group-and-outcome combination with the size it would have if group and outcome were unrelated. It adds copies of positive examples from the disadvantaged group and negative examples from the favoured group, and removes negative examples from the disadvantaged group and positive examples from the favoured group, always starting with those closest to the decision boundary. Labels are never changed, so a standard classifier can learn from the rebalanced set.

example_use_cases.description: A graduate recruiter's historical shortlisting data shows women were shortlisted less often than men with similar scores. The team trains a ranking model, then copies the shortlisted women and rejected men closest to the decision boundary and removes the rejected women and shortlisted men closest to it, until the shortlisting rates match. No label is changed, and the production model is trained on the resampled set.

A bank training a loan-approval model on ten years of decisions finds that applicants under 25 were approved far less often than older applicants. Compliance wants the recorded decisions left untouched, so the model team resamples the training set until approval rates match across age groups and keeps the original labels as the record of what was decided.

limitations.description: Duplicating examples invites overfitting, and removing them discards information. The method copies the same borderline examples and drops others, so a model may memorise duplicates or lose cases it needed, which matters most when the training set is small or many changes are needed.

It assumes the whole gap in positive rates between groups is discrimination. It resamples until outcome and group are unrelated, even where part of the gap has a legitimate explanation such as differing experience, and the original authors note that this constraint is often too strong.

The result depends on a ranking model learned from the same biased data. The ranker decides which examples count as borderline, so a weak or biased ranker copies and removes the wrong ones, and in the original experiments the method worked best with unstable learners such as decision trees.

It handles one binary protected attribute and a binary outcome. Gender and ethnicity together are not covered, so resampling for one attribute can leave intersectional groups unbalanced, and the authors call multiple combined attributes a harder open problem.

Fairness is achieved on the training data, not guaranteed on new data. In the original Census Income experiment with decision trees, discrimination fell from about 16 to about 3 per cent, not to zero, and the protected attribute must be recorded for every training example.

techniques.name: Prejudice Remover Regulariser
techniques.description: The Prejudice Remover Regulariser, proposed by Kamishima and colleagues (2012), trains a classifier with an extra fairness penalty that discourages its predictions from carrying information about a sensitive attribute such as gender or race. The penalty approximates the 'mutual information' between the predicted label and the sensitive attribute, which measures how much knowing one tells you about the other. It is added to the usual training objective, so the model is pushed to fit the labels while keeping that dependence low. The authors built it into logistic regression and describe it as applicable to other classifiers that output probabilities. One parameter sets the penalty strength, so a practitioner can trade some accuracy for a smaller dependence on the sensitive attribute.

example_use_cases.description: A lender's modelling team retrains its logistic-regression credit-scoring model with the prejudice remover penalty, using applicant gender as the sensitive attribute. It tries several penalty strengths and records how far approval decisions still depend on gender and how much predictive accuracy is lost at each, so the credit committee can choose the strength it will accept.

A health-system analytics team building a postpartum depression risk model on insurance claims trains it with the penalty, with race as the sensitive attribute. It compares disparate impact and equal opportunity difference with an unpenalised model on the same held-out data, to decide whether the penalised model is good enough or another bias-reduction method is needed.

A university building a model to flag students for early support trains it with the penalty so that flags depend less on gender. The team reports to the student-support board how much accuracy the chosen strength costs, and how far the difference in flag rates between genders shrinks, before the model is used.

limitations.description: The penalty strength has to be tuned, and no setting is right in advance. In the original experiments on census income data, the strongest penalty tested cut the difference in positive-prediction rates between men and women from 0.19 to 0.01, but accuracy fell from about 85% to 77%. The choice is a judgement about how much accuracy to give up.

The sensitive attribute is an input to the model at training and at prediction time, in the original method and in the AIF360 implementation. The technique cannot be used where the attribute is not collected or cannot be used when decisions are made.

The penalty measures only how much predictions depend on the sensitive attribute, not whether errors fall evenly across groups. Where groups really differ in outcome rates in the data, pushing the dependence down misclassifies some individuals to meet the target, and no equal-error-rate guarantee follows.

The original method and the AIF360 implementation cover logistic regression only. Using the penalty with a neural network or another model means deriving and implementing it yourself, and the optimisation was designed for the logistic form.

Reduced dependence is measured on the training sample. With little data, the model can depend on the sensitive attribute more on new cases than on the training data, which the original paper calls underestimation, so the dependence should be re-measured on held-out data.

resources.abstract: The rise of algorithmic decision-making has spawned much research on fair machine learning (ML). Financial institutions use ML for building risk scorecards that support a range of credit-related decisions. Yet, the literature on fair ML in credit scoring is scarce. The paper makes three contributions. First, we revisit statistical fairness criteria and examine their adequacy for credit scoring. Second, we catalog algorithmic options for incorporating fairness goals in the ML model development pipeline. Last, we empirically compare different fairness processors in a profit-oriented credit scoring context using real-world data. The empirical results substantiate the evaluation of fairness measures, identify suitable options to implement fair credit scoring, and clarify the profit-fairness trade-off in lending decisions. We find that multiple fairness criteria can be approximately satisfied at once and recommend separation as a proper criterion for measuring the fairness of a scorecard. We also find fair in-processors to deliver a good balance between profit and fairness and show that algorithmic discrimination can be reduced to a reasonable level at a relatively low cost. The codes corresponding to the paper are available on GitHub.

resources.title: Evaluating Fairness Strategies in Educational Data Mining: A Comparative Study of Bias Mitigation Techniques
resources.abstract: Ensuring fairness in machine learning models applied to educational data is crucial for mitigating biases that can reinforce systemic inequities. This paper compares various fairness-enhancing algorithms across preprocessing, in-processing, and post-processing stages. Preprocessing methods such as Reweighting, Learning Fair Representations, and Disparate Impact Remover aim to adjust training data to reduce bias before model learning. In-processing techniques, including Adversarial Debiasing and Prejudice Remover, intervene during model training to directly minimize discrimination. Post-processing approaches, such as Equalized Odds Post-Processing, Calibrated Equalized Odds Post-Processing, and Reject Option Classification, adjust model predictions to improve fairness without altering the underlying model. We evaluate these methods on educational datasets, examining their effectiveness in reducing disparate impact while maintaining predictive performance. Our findings highlight tradeoffs between fairness and accuracy, as well as the suitability of different techniques for various educational applications.

The postpartum depression risk model's disparate impact ratio between racial groups is closer to 1 than that of the unpenalised model on the same held-out data.

The student-support flagging model's flag rates differ less between genders than those of the unpenalised baseline on held-out students, and the accuracy lost is reported to the student-support board.

techniques.name: Meta Fair Classifier
techniques.description: The meta fair classifier is a general-purpose training algorithm for fair classification. The user chooses a fairness metric, such as the statistical rate (each group's share of favourable outcomes) or the false discovery rate (the share of positive predictions that are wrong), and a target between 0 and 1 for how close to equal the groups' values must be. From labelled training examples that include the protected attribute, the algorithm fits a model of the data, solves a series of constrained optimisation problems, and returns the most accurate classifier that meets the target. It trains a new classifier rather than adjusting an existing one. The original paper proves the result comes close to the best classifier that meets the target, up to the error in the fitted model of the data.

example_use_cases.description: A recruitment platform trains a shortlisting classifier with a statistical-rate target of 0.8, so that the selection rate for any gender group is at least 80% of the highest group's rate, and measures how much accuracy it gives up to reach that target.

A probation service building a recidivism risk classifier constrains false discovery rate parity, so that among people flagged as high risk, the share who do not go on to reoffend is similar across racial groups.

A hospital building a classifier for heart conditions constrains false discovery rate parity, so that false alarms, which send people for unnecessary medical attention, do not fall more heavily on women than on men.

limitations.description: It is a self-contained learner, not a wrapper. It cannot adjust a model you already run, and the paper lists extension to other classifier types as future work. It also needs the protected attribute for every training example, and teams must be willing to replace their model with the one it produces.

The AIF360 implementation supports only statistical rate and false discovery rate, and raises an error for any other metric. The paper's framework covers more, but other criteria, such as equalised odds, mean extra implementation work or choosing a different technique.

The guarantee depends on how well the fitted model of the data matches the real distribution, and the paper's bound carries error terms for any mismatch. In its experiments, a simple fitted model gave lower accuracy than competing methods at the same fairness level.
Results can vary from run to run. In a credit-scoring comparison, repeated runs sometimes missed the fairness target, which made averaging the results unusable.

The method solves a separate constrained optimisation problem for each value on a grid set by the tolerance, and the number multiplies for each additional fairness metric constrained at once. Combining several criteria quickly makes training slow.

resources.title: Classification with Fairness Constraints
resources.abstract: Developing classification algorithms that are fair with respect to sensitive attributes of the data is an important problem due to the increased deployment of classification algorithms in societal contexts. Several recent works have focused on studying classification with respect to specific fairness metrics, modeled the corresponding fair classification problem as constrained optimization problems, and developed tailored algorithms to solve them. Despite this, there still remain important metrics for which there are no fair classifiers with theoretical guarantees; primarily because the resulting optimization problem is non-convex. The main contribution of this paper is a meta-algorithm for classification that can take as input a general class of fairness constraints with respect to multiple non-disjoint and multi-valued sensitive attributes, and which comes with provable guarantees. In particular, our algorithm can handle non-convex "linear fractional" constraints (which includes fairness constraints such as predictive parity) for which no prior algorithm was known. Key to our results is an algorithm for a family of classification problems with convex constraints along with a reduction from classification problems with linear fractional constraints to this family. Empirically, we observe that our algorithm is fast, can achieve near-perfect fairness with respect to various fairness metrics, and the loss in accuracy due to the imposed fairness constraints is often small.

resources.title: Algorithmic decision making methods for fair credit scoring
resources.abstract: The effectiveness of machine learning in evaluating the creditworthiness of loan applicants has been demonstrated for a long time. However, there is concern that the use of automated decision-making processes may result in unequal treatment of groups or individuals, potentially leading to discriminatory outcomes. This paper seeks to address this issue by evaluating the effectiveness of 12 leading bias mitigation methods across 5 different fairness metrics, as well as assessing their accuracy and potential profitability for financial institutions. Through our analysis, we have identified the challenges associated with achieving fairness while maintaining accuracy and profitabiliy, and have highlighted both the most successful and least successful mitigation methods. Ultimately, our research serves to bridge the gap between experimental machine learning and its practical applications in the finance industry.

resources.title: Fairness in credit scoring: Assessment, implementation and profit implications
resources.abstract: The rise of algorithmic decision-making has spawned much research on fair machine learning (ML). Financial institutions use ML for building risk scorecards that support a range of credit-related decisions. Yet, the literature on fair ML in credit scoring is scarce. The paper makes three contributions. First, we revisit statistical fairness criteria and examine their adequacy for credit scoring. Second, we catalog algorithmic options for incorporating fairness goals in the ML model development pipeline. Last, we empirically compare different fairness processors in a profit-oriented credit scoring context using real-world data. The empirical results substantiate the evaluation of fairness measures, identify suitable options to implement fair credit scoring, and clarify the profit-fairness trade-off in lending decisions. We find that multiple fairness criteria can be approximately satisfied at once and recommend separation as a proper criterion for measuring the fairness of a scorecard. We also find fair in-processors to deliver a good balance between profit and fairness and show that algorithmic discrimination can be reduced to a reasonable level at a relatively low cost. The codes corresponding to the paper are available on GitHub.

sample_claims.text: On held-out data, the shortlisting classifier's selection rate for each gender group is at least 80% of the highest group's rate.

techniques.name: Exponentiated Gradient Reduction
techniques.description: Exponentiated gradient reduction trains a classifier that satisfies a chosen fairness criterion, such as demographic parity (equal rates of favourable outcomes across groups) or equalised odds (equal error rates across groups), while keeping error as low as it can. It reduces the problem to a series of ordinary training runs on the same data, each with different example weights. Between runs, a multiplicative update, the exponentiated gradient step, increases the weight on fairness constraints that are currently violated, and a standard classifier is retrained on the reweighted data. The output is a randomised classifier, a weighted mix of the classifiers trained along the way, with one drawn at random for each prediction. The original paper proves that its error and its fairness violation come close to the best achievable, up to a tolerance the user sets and the statistical error from a finite training set.

example_use_cases.description: A recruitment team trains a shortlisting model under a demographic parity constraint so that selection rates are equal across gender groups, and sweeps the method's tolerance setting to see how much accuracy each step towards equality costs.

A justice agency building a recidivism risk model trains a logistic regression under a demographic parity constraint on race, then compares accuracy and fairness metrics against the unconstrained model on the same data before deciding whether to deploy it.

A lender trying equalised odds, true-positive-rate difference and demographic parity as constraints on its credit-scoring model picks the one that gives the best balance of accuracy and profit on its own data, since the best choice differs between datasets.

limitations.description: The guarantees assume the base learner can solve each weighted training problem close to exactly. Real learners only approximate this, so the stated bounds on error and fairness violation are approximate in practice. The learner must also accept per-example weights, which rules out some model types.

The result is a randomised mix of classifiers, so the same input can receive different predictions on repeat requests. This is hard to defend where decisions must be repeatable, as in appeals or audits.

Needs the protected attribute for every training example, although not at prediction time. It enforces one fairness criterion at a time, and the original paper leaves trading off several criteria as an open problem.

Each round retrains the base model, and the number of rounds needed grows with the square of the inverse of the tolerance, so halving the tolerance roughly quadruples training cost. Large datasets or slow models make tight tolerances expensive.

Constraint violation is controlled only up to sampling error, which is larger for small groups. In one credit-scoring comparison the best-performing constraint differed between datasets, so the right criterion has to be found by experiment on the data in hand.

resources.title: A Reductions Approach to Fair Classification
resources.abstract: We present a systematic approach for achieving fairness in a binary classification setting. While we focus on two well-known quantitative definitions of fairness, our approach encompasses many other previously studied definitions as special cases. The key idea is to reduce fair classification to a sequence of cost-sensitive classification problems, whose solutions yield a randomized classifier with the lowest (empirical) error subject to the desired constraints. We introduce two reductions that work for any representation of the cost-sensitive classifier and compare favorably to prior baselines on a variety of data sets, while overcoming several of their disadvantages.

resources.title: A fairness-focused approach to recidivism prediction: implications for accuracy, trust, and equity
resources.abstract: Fairness in AI has emerged as a critical priority, particularly in high-stakes domains like criminal justice, where algorithmic decisions profoundly affect individuals and demographic groups. This study addresses persistent challenges of bias in recidivism prediction by evaluating the integrated application of fairness-enhancing techniques across the AI pipeline. Specifically, we analyze the integrated use of Reweighing, Adversarial Learning, Disparate Impact Remover, Exponentiated Gradient Reduction, Reject Option Classification, and Equalized Odds optimization. These methods are assessed using key fairness metrics, Statistical Parity Difference (SPD), Disparate Impact (DI), Equal Opportunity Difference (EOD), and Predictive Equality Difference (PED), on two real-world recidivism datasets: COMPAS, a well-known publicly available dataset, and RisCanvi, a curated English dataset derived from a publicly available Spanish dataset. Our findings reveal trade-offs between fairness improvements and predictive accuracy, with fairness performance varying across integrated mitigation strategies. While individual techniques often fall short of effectively reducing bias, their integration across pre-processing, in-processing, and post-processing stages demonstrates a more comprehensive and robust capacity to address fairness concerns. In some instances, fairness mitigation strategies exacerbate disparities instead of reducing them, highlighting the complexity of achieving equitable AI outcomes. Some methods struggle with specific datasets, leading to worsened SPD, DI, EOD, or PED values, potentially reinforcing biases rather than eliminating them. Using multi-objective and bi-objective optimization frameworks, we identify optimal configurations that balance fairness and accuracy, contributing to a deeper understanding of fairness–accuracy trade-offs in AI systems. This study makes a novel contribution by systematically evaluating multi-phase fairness integration in recidivism prediction, bridging critical gaps in the literature. However, our results also underscore the risks of ineffective or counterproductive fairness interventions when not carefully tailored. Our findings highlight the necessity of tailoring bias mitigation strategies to specific datasets and contexts, providing actionable insights for developing equitable, diverse, and inclusive AI systems that are fair and reliable in the criminal justice system.

On held-out data, the shortlisting model's selection rates differ between gender groups by no more than the agreed tolerance.
The recidivism model's true-positive and false-positive rates differ across racial groups by less than the agreed tolerance, and the accuracy cost against the unconstrained model is reported.

techniques.name: Learning Adversarially Fair and Transferable Representations
techniques.description: Learning Adversarially Fair and Transferable Representations (LAFTR) trains an encoder that turns each record into a representation, a vector of learned features, from which a protected attribute is hard to recover, so that models later built on that representation by other parties, including for prediction tasks not known in advance, also treat groups fairly. It was designed for a data owner who shares encoded data with downstream model builders and cannot control how they train. During training, the encoder, a decoder that reconstructs the input and a classifier for the original task play against an adversary network that tries to predict the protected attribute from the representation; the encoder is updated to defeat the adversary while keeping the information the other two need. The adversary's objective is matched to demographic parity, equalised odds or equal opportunity, and the authors prove that an optimal adversary's objective bounds that unfairness measure for any classifier trained on the representation (for the two error-rate measures the adversary also sees the labels used in training, so the attribute is hidden given the label, and the bound is with respect to those labels). The output is a frozen encoder, delivered with the accuracy and fairness of classifiers trained on top of it.

example_use_cases.description: A data marketplace that supplies customer records to advertisers wants assurance that the targeting models advertisers build will not show offers to men and women at different rates. It trains LAFTR with the demographic parity adversary, releases only the encoded features, and audits a sample of advertisers' models for the gap in positive rates and for how well a fresh classifier can recover gender from the released features.

A health insurer's data team shares encoded claims and prescription data with external analytics suppliers who build their own risk models. It trains LAFTR with an equalised-odds adversary on a comorbidity-risk task, with patients aged 70 or over as the protected group, then measures error-rate gaps for classifiers trained on held-out condition-prediction tasks, because fairness on those new tasks has to be measured rather than assumed.

A hospital imaging research group compares LAFTR with standard training for a chest X-ray triage classifier, with patient sex as the protected attribute and the model-selection rule fixed in advance, to decide whether debiasing the representation narrows the gap in error rates enough to justify its extra training cost.

limitations.description: The fairness bound holds only for an optimal adversary. A weak or under-trained adversary underestimates how much protected information the representation still carries, so downstream models can be less fair than training suggested; the authors report uneven results in places, which they attribute to unstable adversarial training. Audit downstream models directly, including with a fresh classifier trained to recover the protected attribute from the representation.

Transfer to new tasks is not guaranteed for the error-rate criteria. The equalised-odds and equal-opportunity adversaries use the original task's labels, so fairness on a new task with different labels is an empirical result: in the paper's health-data experiment LAFTR was the fairest method on seven of ten transfer tasks, and the authors leave open which tasks transfer fairly.

As formulated, it handles one binary protected attribute and a binary task label; intersectional groups, several attributes or multi-class outcomes need an extension. Training needs the protected attribute and, for the error-rate criteria, the task labels. In the paper's experiments the encoder also took the protected attribute as input, so it is needed whenever new records are encoded; no results are reported without it.

Measured gains can be small in practice. MEDFAIR, a peer-reviewed benchmark of eleven bias-mitigation methods including LAFTR on medical imaging datasets, found the methods did not significantly improve fairness over standard training when trained and tested on the same task, including across datasets (it did not test transfer to new tasks), and that the model-selection criterion changed fairness results substantially. Compare against a standard model under a selection rule stated in advance.

Up to four networks (encoder, decoder, classifier, adversary) are trained against each other, with three weights balancing accuracy, reconstruction and fairness. The paper argues reconstruction is needed for transfer and used different weights for fair classification (accuracy 1, reconstruction 0) and for transfer (accuracy 0, reconstruction 1), so settings do not carry over. The 2018 reference code pins Python 3.6 and TensorFlow 1.9; reimplementations sit inside research benchmarks.

resources.title: Learning Adversarially Fair and Transferable Representations
resources.abstract: In this paper, we advocate for representation learning as the key to mitigating unfair prediction outcomes downstream. Motivated by a scenario where learned representations are used by third parties with unknown objectives, we propose and explore adversarial representation learning as a natural method of ensuring those parties act fairly. We connect group fairness (demographic parity, equalized odds, and equal opportunity) to different adversarial objectives. Through worst-case theoretical guarantees and experimental validation, we show that the choice of this objective is crucial to fair prediction. Furthermore, we present the first in-depth experimental demonstration of fair transfer learning and demonstrate empirically that our learned representations admit fair predictions on new tasks while maintaining utility, an essential goal of fair representation learning.

resources.title: MEDFAIR: Benchmarking Fairness for Medical Imaging
resources.abstract: A multitude of work has shown that machine learning-based medical diagnosis systems can be biased against certain subgroups of people. This has motivated a growing number of bias mitigation algorithms that aim to address fairness issues in machine learning. However, it is difficult to compare their effectiveness in medical imaging for two reasons. First, there is little consensus on the criteria to assess fairness. Second, existing bias mitigation algorithms are developed under different settings, e.g., datasets, model selection strategies, backbones, and fairness metrics, making a direct comparison and evaluation based on existing results impossible. In this work, we introduce MEDFAIR, a framework to benchmark the fairness of machine learning models for medical imaging. MEDFAIR covers eleven algorithms from various categories, nine datasets from different imaging modalities, and three model selection criteria. Through extensive experiments, we find that the under-studied issue of model selection criterion can have a significant impact on fairness outcomes; while in contrast, state-of-the-art bias mitigation algorithms do not significantly improve fairness outcomes over empirical risk minimization (ERM) in both in-distribution and out-of-distribution settings. We evaluate fairness from various perspectives and make recommendations for different medical application scenarios that require different ethical principles. Our framework provides a reproducible and easy-to-use entry point for the development and evaluation of future bias mitigation algorithms in deep learning. Code is available at https://github.com/ys-zong/MEDFAIR.

sample_claims.text: Classifiers trained by external parties on the released representation show a demographic parity difference below the agreed threshold on every downstream task audited.

A classifier trained to recover the protected attribute from the representation released under the demographic parity objective does no better than always predicting the majority group, within an agreed margin.
The fairness of downstream risk models built on the shared encoded data was measured on each new prediction task rather than assumed from the task the encoder was trained on.
Under a model-selection rule fixed in advance, the debiased imaging model narrows the gap in error rates between patient groups relative to standard training by a measured margin.

techniques.name: Multi-Accuracy Boosting
techniques.description: Multi-accuracy boosting is a post-processing method that corrects a trained classifier's systematic errors on subgroups of people, without retraining it. It needs only the classifier's predictions and a small labelled validation set. An auditor, usually a simple model such as a ridge regression or a shallow decision tree, learns to predict where the classifier's predictions are consistently too high or too low, which finds overlapping subgroups without anyone naming them in advance. Each round fits a small correction for the worst subgroup, as in boosting, and the loop stops when the auditor can find no subgroup whose average error exceeds a chosen tolerance. The result is multi-accuracy, meaning unbiased predictions on every subgroup the auditor can identify, which is not the same as equal accuracy across groups, and the audit itself reports where the original model failed.

example_use_cases.description: A hospital buys a black-box diagnostic model it cannot retrain. Its data team holds a small labelled sample of local patients and runs the audit, which finds that predictions are systematically too low for older women. The team post-processes the model until no subgroup the auditor can find exceeds the agreed error tolerance, then checks that groups the model already served well did not get worse.

A lender uses a vendor's credit-risk model, and its data holds no sensitive attributes. A risk analyst audits the model on a labelled sample of recent applications with a decision-tree auditor, which finds subgroups defined by ordinary features where the errors concentrate. The correction is applied until those subgroups' average error falls within tolerance.

limitations.description: The guarantee covers only subgroups the auditor can identify from the features. If a group's errors follow a pattern too complex for the auditor, or the features carry little trace of group membership, the audit will pass the model while that group is still poorly served.

Multi-accuracy bounds the average prediction error within each identified subgroup. It does not equalise error rates, so large gaps can remain. In the original paper's face-image test, error after correction was still 12.5% for dark-skinned women against 1.0% for light-skinned women.

It needs a labelled validation sample that represents the population and is large enough for the groups of concern. The guarantee for a subgroup weakens as the subgroup's share of the sample shrinks, so rare groups are protected least.

Corrections are fitted on the small audit sample, so too many rounds or an over-flexible auditor will start fitting noise and can make performance worse on new data. The mcboost documentation says its calibration 'tends to overfit' and suggests a smaller step size or fewer iterations.

The method corrects errors against the labels in the audit sample, so it cannot repair bias already built into those labels, such as past decisions recorded as outcomes. A fairer-looking score then still reproduces the earlier pattern.

resources.abstract:
Implements Multi-Calibration Boosting (2018) <https://proceedings.mlr.press/v80/hebert-johnson18a.html> and
    Multi-Accuracy Boosting (2019) <arXiv:1805.12317> for the multi-calibration of a machine learning models prediction.
    MCBoost' updates predictions for sub-groups in an iterative fashion in order to mitigate biases like poor calibration or large accuracy differences across subgroups.
    Multi-Calibration works best in scenarios where the underlying data & labels are unbiased, but resulting models are.
    This is often the case, e.g. when an algorithm fits a majority population while ignoring or under-fitting minority populations.

resources.abstract: Given the increasing usage of automated prediction systems in the context of high-stakes decisions, a growing body of research focuses on methods for detecting and mitigating biases in algorithmic decision-making.One important framework to audit for and mitigate biases in predictions is that of Multi-Calibration, introduced by Hebert-Johnson et al. (2018).The underlying fairness notion, Multi-Calibration, promotes the idea of multi-group fairness and requires calibrated predictions not only for marginal populations, but also for subpopulations that may be defined by complex intersections of many attributes.A simpler variant of Multi-Calibration, referred to as Multi-Accuracy, requires unbiased predictions for large collections of subpopulations.Hebert-Johnson et al. (2018) proposed a boosting-style algorithm for learning multi-calibrated predictors.Kim et al. (2019) demonstrated how to turn this algorithm into a post-processing strategy to achieve multi-accuracy, demonstrating empirical effectiveness across various domains.This package provides a stable implementation of the multi-calibration algorithm, called MCBoost.In contrast to other Fair ML approaches, MC-Boost does not harm the overall utility of a prediction model, but rather aims at improving calibration and accuracy for large sets of subpopulations post-training.MCBoost comes with strong theoretical guarantees, which have been explored formally in Hebert-Johnson et al.

resources.title: Multiaccuracy
resources.abstract: Prediction systems are successfully deployed in applications ranging from disease diagnosis, to predicting credit worthiness, to image recognition. Even when the overall accuracy is high, these systems may exhibit systematic biases that harm specific subpopulations; such biases may arise inadvertently due to underrepresentation in the data used to train a machine-learning model, or as the result of intentional malicious discrimination. We develop a rigorous framework of *multiaccuracy* auditing and post-processing to ensure accurate predictions across *identifiable subgroups*. Our algorithm, MULTIACCURACY-BOOST, works in any setting where we have black-box access to a predictor and a relatively small set of labeled data for auditing; importantly, this black-box framework allows for improved fairness and accountability of predictions, even when the predictor is minimally transparent. We prove that MULTIACCURACY-BOOST converges efficiently and show that if the initial model is accurate on an identifiable subgroup, then the post-processed model will be also. We experimentally demonstrate the effectiveness of the approach to improve the accuracy among minority subgroups in diverse applications (image classification, finance, population health). Interestingly, MULTIACCURACY-BOOST can improve subpopulation accuracy (e.g. for "black women") even when the sensitive features (e.g. "race", "gender") are not given to the algorithm explicitly.

resources.title: Calibration for the (Computationally-Identifiable) Masses
resources.abstract: As algorithms increasingly inform and influence decisions made about individuals, it becomes increasingly important to address concerns that these algorithms might be discriminatory. The output of an algorithm can be discriminatory for many reasons, most notably: (1) the data used to train the algorithm might be biased (in various ways) to favor certain populations over others; (2) the analysis of this training data might inadvertently or maliciously introduce biases that are not borne out in the data. This work focuses on the latter concern. We develop and study multicalbration -- a new measure of algorithmic fairness that aims to mitigate concerns about discrimination that is introduced in the process of learning a predictor from data. Multicalibration guarantees accurate (calibrated) predictions for every subpopulation that can be identified within a specified class of computations. We think of the class as being quite rich; in particular, it can contain many overlapping subgroups of a protected group. We show that in many settings this strong notion of protection from discrimination is both attainable and aligned with the goal of obtaining accurate predictions. Along the way, we present new algorithms for learning a multicalibrated predictor, study the computational complexity of this task, and draw new connections to computational learning models such as agnostic learning.

techniques.name: Threshold Optimiser
techniques.description: Threshold Optimiser is a post-processing method, introduced by Hardt, Price and Srebro (2016), that adjusts a trained classifier's decisions to meet a group fairness criterion without retraining it, most often equalised odds (equal true positive and false positive rates in every group) or equal opportunity (equal true positive rates only). It uses a labelled validation set that records each person's group, and traces each group's ROC curve, which shows the true and false positive rates the model's score gives at every possible cut-off. It then chooses a separate cut-off for each group that keeps accuracy, or another chosen objective, as high as the criterion allows. Equalised odds usually cannot be met with one cut-off per group, so each group's decision is randomised between two cut-offs with fixed probabilities. The output is a rule that needs each person's group at prediction time, and if the model gives only yes/no predictions, a small linear optimisation sets the probability of flipping each prediction instead.

example_use_cases.description: A lender's model validation team applies the method to an existing credit-scoring model, choosing a separate approval cut-off for each racial group so that applicants who go on to repay are approved at the same rate in every group (equal opportunity). It compares the expected profit of that rule with a single cut-off and with an equalised-odds rule before recommending which one the credit committee should adopt.

A hospital system's data science team adjusts the alert threshold of an unplanned-readmission model separately for each race and ethnicity group, so that patients who are later readmitted are flagged at similar rates across groups. The change is accepted only because overall accuracy and daily alert volume stay within limits agreed with clinicians before the adjustment was made.

A public agency licenses a pre-trial risk tool that returns only high or low labels, with no access to scores or retraining. Using a held-out set of past cases with known outcomes, it derives the label-flipping rule that gives equal true and false positive rates across racial groups, and reports to its oversight board how many decisions the rule would change and how much accuracy it costs.

An HR analytics team piloting a CV-scoring model runs the method under equal opportunity and under equalised odds on its validation data, to show the selection panel what each criterion costs in accuracy and how many shortlisting decisions it would change. The comparison is the evidence for which fairness criterion the panel signs off before deployment.

limitations.description: The cut-off depends on the person's group, so the protected attribute must be available at the moment of decision (Fairlearn's predict requires it). Where the attribute is not collected, or where applying different cut-offs by group could count as direct discrimination or disparate treatment, which Fairlearn's own guide flags for EU and US law, the rule may be unusable in deployment even though it works in validation.

Meeting equalised odds exactly usually requires randomisation, so two people with the same score and group can receive different decisions, and Fairlearn notes that some solutions give a non-zero chance of a positive decision whatever the score. Where decisions must be reproducible or explained to the individual, such as credit refusals, this can rule the method out or force a relaxed constraint.

Under equalised odds every group's error rates are held to what the hardest-to-predict group's ROC curve allows; Hardt et al. note such a classifier must classify everyone as poorly as the hardest group. In their credit case study it kept about 80% of maximum profit against about 93% for equal opportunity, and Fairlearn warns of levelling down: worse performance for the better-served group with no gain for the worse-served one.

Cut-offs are estimated from a finite labelled sample in which group membership is known, and the original analysis sets sampling error aside. Small groups give unstable cut-offs, and rates equalised on the validation set drift when the population or the model's score distribution changes, so the cut-offs must be re-estimated and the equalised rates monitored after deployment.

Equalised odds generally conflicts with calibration within groups: Pleiss et al. (2017) show that when groups have different base rates and the predictor is imperfect, calibration is compatible with at most one equal-error-rate constraint. A team that must show both equal error rates and calibrated risk for each group cannot obtain both from this method, and relaxing to equal opportunity does not by itself keep the original score calibrated.

resources.title: Equality of Opportunity in Supervised Learning
resources.abstract: We propose a criterion for discrimination against a specified sensitive attribute in supervised learning, where the goal is to predict some target based on available features. Assuming data about the predictor, target, and membership in the protected group are available, we show how to optimally adjust any learned predictor so as to remove discrimination according to our definition. Our framework also improves incentives by shifting the cost of poor classification from disadvantaged groups to the decision maker, who can respond by improving the classification accuracy.   In line with other studies, our notion is oblivious: it depends only on the joint statistics of the predictor, the target and the protected attribute, but not on interpretation of individualfeatures. We study the inherent limits of defining and identifying biases based on such oblivious measures, outlining what can and cannot be inferred from different oblivious tests.   We illustrate our notion using a case study of FICO credit scores.

resources.title: Group-Aware Threshold Adaptation for Fair Classification
resources.abstract: The fairness in machine learning is getting increasing attention, as its applications in different fields continue to expand and diversify. To mitigate the discriminated model behaviors between different demographic groups, we introduce a novel post-processing method to optimize over multiple fairness constraints through group-aware threshold adaptation. We propose to learn adaptive classification thresholds for each demographic group by optimizing the confusion matrix estimated from the probability distribution of a classification model output. As we only need an estimated probability distribution of model output instead of the classification model structure, our post-processing model can be applied to a wide range of classification models and improve fairness in a model-agnostic manner and ensure privacy. This even allows us to post-process existing fairness methods to further improve the trade-off between accuracy and fairness. Moreover, our model has low computational cost. We provide rigorous theoretical analysis on the convergence of our optimization algorithm and the trade-off between accuracy and fairness of our method. Our method theoretically enables a better upper bound in near optimality than existing method under same condition. Experimental results demonstrate that our method outperforms state-of-the-art methods and obtains the result that is closest to the theoretical accuracy-fairness trade-off boundary.

resources.abstract: Algorithmic bias occurs when predictive model performance varies meaningfully across sociodemographic classes, exacerbating systemic healthcare disparities. We evaluated differences in subgroup performance across race/ethnicity, sex, language, and insurance using equal opportunity difference (EOD), a metric comparing false negative rates. The most biased classes (race/ethnicity for asthma, insurance for readmission) were targeted for mitigation using threshold adjustment, which adjusts subgroup thresholds to minimize EOD, and reject option classification, which re-classifies scores near the threshold by subgroup. Successful mitigation was defined as 1) absolute subgroup EODs <5 percentage points, 2) accuracy reduction <10%, and 3) alert rate change <20%. Threshold adjustment met these criteria; reject option classification did not. We introduce a Supplementary Playbook outlining our approach for low-resource bias mitigation.

techniques.name: Reject Option Classification
techniques.description: Reject Option Classification is a post-processing method, proposed by Kamiran and colleagues (2012), that changes some of a trained classifier's decisions to reduce unfair outcomes between groups, without retraining it. It defines a 'critical region' around the decision boundary, where the predicted probability is close to 50 per cent and the model is least sure. Inside that region it gives the favourable outcome to people from the disadvantaged group and the unfavourable outcome to people from the advantaged group, whatever the model predicted, and decisions outside it are left alone. The width of the region is searched on a labelled validation set, so that a chosen fairness measure, such as statistical parity difference or equal opportunity difference, falls within a set bound while accuracy stays as high as possible. The method needs each person's group at prediction time.

example_use_cases.description: A graduate recruiter's data team has a CV-scoring model whose scores near the shortlisting cut-off are the least certain. Using a labelled validation set, it searches for the narrowest band around that cut-off that brings the difference in shortlisting rates between men and women within five percentage points, and reports how many candidates' outcomes the band changes.

A hospital data science team tests the method on an unplanned-readmission alert model to narrow the gap in missed-readmission rates between insurance groups. It adopts the change only if the gap falls below five percentage points while accuracy drops by under 10 per cent and alert volume changes by under 20 per cent, and drops the method if any limit is missed.

A court service reviewing a pre-trial risk score applies the method with race as the group attribute, so that defendants whose scores sit close to the high-risk cut-off are not decided by small score differences that may reflect the model's bias. The service reports to its oversight body how many decisions the band changes, in which direction, and what it costs in accuracy.

limitations.description: Needs a model that outputs scores, because the critical region is defined on them, so a model that outputs only yes/no labels cannot be used. The scores need not be calibrated probabilities, but if they are poorly calibrated or bunched together, the wrong people fall inside the region.

Inside the region the outcome is set by group membership, so the method needs each person's group at decision time and treats people differently by group. This may be unlawful or unacceptable in some settings, such as hiring or lending, and the group attribute must be available when decisions are made.

A person from the advantaged group with a borderline score receives the unfavourable outcome, and one from the other group the favourable outcome, whatever their individual merit. A wider band closes more of the fairness gap but sets more decisions by group instead of by score, so accuracy falls as the band widens.

Cannot address bias in confident predictions outside the region. The method assumes discrimination is concentrated near the decision boundary, so where a model is confidently wrong about one group, the adjustment leaves those decisions as they are.

The band is chosen by grid search on a labelled validation set against a fairness bound (the AIF360 default is plus or minus 0.05). A small or unrepresentative validation set gives an unreliable band, and if no setting meets the bound the search returns a fallback that may not be acceptable.

resources.title: Decision Theory for Discrimination-Aware Classification
resources.abstract: Social discrimination (e.g., against females) arising from data mining techniques is a growing concern worldwide. In recent years, several methods have been proposed for making classifiers learned over discriminatory data discrimination-aware. However, these methods suffer from two major shortcomings: (1) They require either modifying the discriminatory data or tweaking a specific classification algorithm and (2) They are not flexible w.r.t. discrimination control and multiple sensitive attribute handling. In this paper, we present two solutions for discrimination-aware classification that neither require data modification nor classifier tweaking. Our first and second solutions exploit, respectively, the reject option of probabilistic classifier(s) and the disagreement region of general classifier ensembles to reduce discrimination. We relate both solutions with decision theory for better understanding of the process. Our experiments using real-world datasets demonstrate that our solutions outperform existing state-of-the-art methods, especially at low discrimination which is a significant advantage. The superior performance coupled with flexible control over discrimination and easy applicability to multiple sensitive attributes makes our solutions an important step forward in practical discrimination-aware classification.

resources.title: Exploiting reject option in classification for social discrimination control
resources.abstract: Social discrimination is said to occur when an unfavorable decision for an individual is influenced by her membership to certain protected groups such as females and minority ethnic groups. Such discriminatory decisions often exist in historical data. Despite recent works in discrimination-aware data mining, there remains the need for robust, yet easily usable, methods for discrimination control. In this paper, we utilize reject option in classification, a general decision theoretic framework for handling instances whose labels are uncertain, for modeling and controlling discriminatory decisions. Specifically, this framework permits a formal treatment of the intuition that instances close to the decision boundary are more likely to be discriminated in a dataset. Based on this framework, we present three different solutions for discrimination-aware classification. The first solution invokes probabilistic rejection in single or multiple probabilistic classifiers while the second solution relies upon ensemble rejection in classifier ensembles. The third solution integrates one of the first two solutions with situation testing which is a procedure commonly used in the court of law. All solutions are easy to use and provide strong justifications for the decisions. We evaluate our solutions extensively on four real-world datasets and compare their performances with previously proposed discrimination-aware classifiers. The results demonstrate the superiority of our solutions in terms of both performance and flexibility of applicability. In particular, our solutions are effective at removing illegal discrimination from the predictions. (C) 2017 Published by Elsevier Inc.

A fairness-focused approach to recidivism prediction: implications for accuracy, trust, and equity
resources.abstract: Fairness in AI has emerged as a critical priority, particularly in high-stakes domains like criminal justice, where algorithmic decisions profoundly affect individuals and demographic groups. This study addresses persistent challenges of bias in recidivism prediction by evaluating the integrated application of fairness-enhancing techniques across the AI pipeline. Specifically, we analyze the integrated use of Reweighing, Adversarial Learning, Disparate Impact Remover, Exponentiated Gradient Reduction, Reject Option Classification, and Equalized Odds optimization. These methods are assessed using key fairness metrics, Statistical Parity Difference (SPD), Disparate Impact (DI), Equal Opportunity Difference (EOD), and Predictive Equality Difference (PED), on two real-world recidivism datasets: COMPAS, a well-known publicly available dataset, and RisCanvi, a curated English dataset derived from a publicly available Spanish dataset. Our findings reveal trade-offs between fairness improvements and predictive accuracy, with fairness performance varying across integrated mitigation strategies. While individual techniques often fall short of effectively reducing bias, their integration across pre-processing, in-processing, and post-processing stages demonstrates a more comprehensive and robust capacity to address fairness concerns. In some instances, fairness mitigation strategies exacerbate disparities instead of reducing them, highlighting the complexity of achieving equitable AI outcomes. Some methods struggle with specific datasets, leading to worsened SPD, DI, EOD, or PED values, potentially reinforcing biases rather than eliminating them. Using multi-objective and bi-objective optimization frameworks, we identify optimal configurations that balance fairness and accuracy, contributing to a deeper understanding of fairness–accuracy trade-offs in AI systems. This study makes a novel contribution by systematically evaluating multi-phase fairness integration in recidivism prediction, bridging critical gaps in the literature. However, our results also underscore the risks of ineffective or counterproductive fairness interventions when not carefully tailored. Our findings highlight the necessity of tailoring bias mitigation strategies to specific datasets and contexts, providing actionable insights for developing equitable, diverse, and inclusive AI systems that are fair and reliable in the criminal justice system.

resources.title: Evaluating Fairness Strategies in Educational Data Mining: A Comparative Study of Bias Mitigation Techniques
resources.abstract: Ensuring fairness in machine learning models applied to educational data is crucial for mitigating biases that can reinforce systemic inequities. This paper compares various fairness-enhancing algorithms across preprocessing, in-processing, and post-processing stages. Preprocessing methods such as Reweighting, Learning Fair Representations, and Disparate Impact Remover aim to adjust training data to reduce bias before model learning. In-processing techniques, including Adversarial Debiasing and Prejudice Remover, intervene during model training to directly minimize discrimination. Post-processing approaches, such as Equalized Odds Post-Processing, Calibrated Equalized Odds Post-Processing, and Reject Option Classification, adjust model predictions to improve fairness without altering the underlying model. We evaluate these methods on educational datasets, examining their effectiveness in reducing disparate impact while maintaining predictive performance. Our findings highlight tradeoffs between fairness and accuracy, as well as the suitability of different techniques for various educational applications.

techniques.name: Calibration with Equality of Opportunity
techniques.description: Calibration with equality of opportunity is a post-processing step that adjusts a classifier's scores so that two groups face the same error rate, in a score-based form of the equal opportunity criterion, while the scores stay calibrated. Calibrated means that, within each group, about 70% of the people given a score of 0.7 really have the outcome. The error rate is computed from the scores rather than from yes-or-no decisions, and for equality of opportunity it is how far, on average, the scores of people who truly have the outcome fall short of 1. Starting from scores already calibrated within each group, the step replaces a randomly chosen share of the scores in the group with the lower error rate by that group's overall rate of the outcome, which makes those predictions less informative until the two error rates match. Calibration is kept at a cost in accuracy for that group, and matching this score-based rate does not guarantee equal true positive rates once a decision threshold is applied.

example_use_cases.description: A hospital team finds that its follow-up screening model gives lower risk scores to women who go on to develop the condition than to men who do. Using a held-out validation set with recorded sex, it adjusts the scores so that this error is equal across the two groups, then measures the accuracy lost by the group whose scores were replaced, to decide whether the model can be released.

A university uses a model to offer extra support to students at risk of dropping out, and wants a score of 0.3 to mean about a 30% dropout rate in every fee-status group. After equalising the error rate across groups, planners plot calibration by group on held-out data to confirm the scores still mean what they say before using them to allocate support places.

limitations.description: The target can be infeasible. If even replacing every score in the lower-error group with that group's base rate leaves its error below the other group's, the two rates cannot be matched while staying calibrated. This happens when the other group's classifier is close to uninformative.

Equality is reached by making predictions worse for the group with the lower error rate, not by improving them for the other group. A random share of that group's scores is replaced by its base rate, and the loss grows with the gap between the groups' base rates.

Calibration can coexist with only one error constraint. Matching the score-based false negative rate leaves false positive rates free to diverge, so one group can face more false alarms, and equalising both while staying calibrated is impossible except in trivial cases.

Because the replaced predictions are chosen at random, two similar people in the same group can receive different outcomes. Those affected may reasonably object that a consequential decision was made by withholding information, which makes the method hard to justify in high-stakes settings.

It needs each person's group attribute when scores are adjusted, labelled held-out data to estimate how many scores to replace, and starting scores already calibrated within each group, which it preserves but cannot create. Where the attribute cannot lawfully be used, or the base model is miscalibrated, the method does not apply.

resources.title: On Fairness and Calibration
resources.abstract: The machine learning community has become increasingly concerned with the potential for bias and discrimination in predictive models. This has motivated a growing line of work on what it means for a classification procedure to be "fair." In this paper, we investigate the tension between minimizing error disparity across different population groups while maintaining calibrated probability estimates. We show that calibration is compatible only with a single error constraint (i.e. equal false-negatives rates across groups), and show that any algorithm that satisfies this relaxation is no better than randomizing a percentage of predictions for an existing classifier. These unsettling findings, which extend and generalize existing results, are empirically confirmed on several datasets.

resources.title: Equality of Opportunity in Supervised Learning
resources.abstract: We propose a criterion for discrimination against a specified sensitive attribute in supervised learning, where the goal is to predict some target based on available features. Assuming data about the predictor, target, and membership in the protected group are available, we show how to optimally adjust any learned predictor so as to remove discrimination according to our definition. Our framework also improves incentives by shifting the cost of poor classification from disadvantaged groups to the decision maker, who can respond by improving the classification accuracy.   In line with other studies, our notion is oblivious: it depends only on the joint statistics of the predictor, the target and the protected attribute, but not on interpretation of individualfeatures. We study the inherent limits of defining and identifying biases based on such oblivious measures, outlining what can and cannot be inferred from different oblivious tests.   We illustrate our notion using a case study of FICO credit scores.

techniques.name: Equal Opportunity Difference
techniques.description: Equal Opportunity Difference checks whether a model is equally likely to give a favourable prediction to the people whose true outcome is favourable, such as loan applicants who would repay, in each demographic group. For each group it calculates the true positive rate: of the people whose true outcome is positive, the share the model also predicts as positive. The score is the gap between two groups' rates, usually the unprivileged group's minus the privileged group's, and 0 means the rates match. Some libraries report the largest gap across all groups instead. The metric follows the equality of opportunity criterion of Hardt, Price and Srebro (2016), and it says nothing about people whose true outcome is negative, so a score of 0 does not show that the model is fair overall.

example_use_cases.description: A bank's model risk team evaluates a loan approval model on past loans with known repayment outcomes. It measures whether applicants who went on to repay were approved at the same rate in each ethnic group, for example 90% for one group against a markedly lower rate for another, before the model is released.

A hospital evaluating a model that flags chest X-rays for suspected pneumonia compares its sensitivity, the share of confirmed cases it flags, between male and female patients and between age bands on a labelled validation set. A gap means affected patients in one group are more likely to be missed, which the clinical safety board weighs before deployment.

A university department checks a model that flags first-year students at risk of dropping out so they can be offered support. Using last year's records, it measures what share of students who actually dropped out were flagged, separately for students who are the first in their family to attend university and for other students.

limitations.description: Only considers true positive rates and ignores false positive rate disparities, potentially allowing discrimination in the form of unequal false alarm rates between groups.

The true outcome labels must be reliable for every group. Where they record past decisions, such as repayment known only for applicants previously approved, or are measured differently between groups, equal true positive rates can reproduce the bias already in the labels.

True positive rates use only the people whose true outcome is positive, so a rare outcome leaves few cases in each group. Gaps can then be noise, and splitting by several attributes at once, such as age within gender, makes this worse.

Closing a gap by lowering one group's decision threshold raises that group's true positive rate but also its false positive rate. Fixing this metric can therefore open a gap in another, and the metric gives no warning when it does.

A score of 0 does not show that the model is fair. The measure uses only predictions, true outcomes and group membership, and Hardt et al. show that situations with different fairness readings can give identical numbers, so a result needs scrutiny of how the outcome was produced.

resources.title: Evaluating algorithmic fairness in the performance of the AHA PREVENT equations versus pooled cohort equations among single-race and multiracial populations
resources.abstract: Background: The performance of AHA PREVENT equation among multiracial individuals has not been assessed. Objective: To assess model performance and fairness of the AHA PREVENT ASCVD (atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease) Equation versus Pooled Cohort Equations (PCE) among single-race and disaggregated multiracial individuals. Method: This is a retrospective cohort data analysis using electronic health record from a 2010-2023 primary care population in a large integrated healthcare system in California. Patient population was restricted to those who are eligible for both the AHA PREVENT base equation and PCE. The primary outcomes were incident ASCVD based on diagnosis codes. We compared measures of model performance as well as algorithmic fairness between PCE and AHA PREVENT, using Disparate Impact (DI), Average Odds Difference (AOD), and Equal Opportunity Difference (EOD). Results: A total of 298,276 patients aged 40-79 years were included, with an average follow-up time of 8 years (SD=3), of which 9% (N=26,761) self-identified as multiracial. In aggregate, 3.9% of multiracial patients developed ASCVD, ranging from 2.9% (Multiple Asian) to 5.4% (Multiracial American Indian/Alaska Native), compared to 4.4% of all single-race patients. Discriminatory performance of the AHA PREVENT ASCVD Equation was good for aggregated multiracial groups (AUC=0.747), ranging from 0.692 (Multiracial Black) to 0.793 (Multiracial Pacific Islander), and was comparable to single-race groups (AUC=0.753). Calibration was generally good among most multiracial groups. However, the AHA PREVENT ASCVD Equation was fairer in its predictive ability when compared to the PCE for all three fairness metrics. Conclusions and relevance: With good discriminatory ability and calibration for single race and multiracial groups, the AHA PREVENT ASCVD Equation provides both more accurate and fairer estimates of ASCVD risk compared to PCE.
