techniques.name: Average Odds Difference
techniques.description: Average Odds Difference summarises how differently a model treats two demographic groups, using two error rates. The true positive rate is the share of people whose true outcome is positive whom the model also predicts as positive. The false positive rate is the share of people whose true outcome is negative whom the model wrongly predicts as positive. The score is the mean of the gap in each rate between the groups, usually the unprivileged group minus the privileged group, so 0 means the two gaps are absent or cancel out. Hardt, Price and Srebro (2016) call the stricter requirement that both gaps are zero equalised odds, and a score near 0 does not guarantee it.

example_use_cases.description: A court-services analytics team audits a pre-trial risk tool on past cases with known outcomes. It reports the average odds difference between racial groups together with the two gaps it averages: how often defendants who later reoffended were rated high risk, and how often those who did not were wrongly rated high risk. The findings go to the oversight board that decides whether the tool stays in use.

A recruitment firm audits its CV-screening tool on past applications whose suitability hiring managers later confirmed. For men and women it compares how often suitable applicants were advanced and how often unsuitable applicants were advanced, and it tracks the average of the two gaps each quarter to decide whether the tool needs retraining.

A hospital compares a sepsis early-warning model across patient ethnic groups before rollout. It checks the share of true sepsis cases flagged and the share of non-sepsis patients falsely flagged, since missed cases and false alarms both carry costs, and uses the average gap to rank candidate models.

limitations.description: Averaging effect can mask important disparities when false positive and true positive rate differences compensate for each other, potentially hiding significant bias in one direction.

The rates are only as trustworthy as the outcome labels, which can differ in quality between groups. Where outcomes are recorded only for people previously approved or hired, such as repayment for granted loans, the gaps describe a selected subset rather than the whole applicant pool. The sensitive attribute must also be available and lawful to use.

When groups differ in how many members truly have the positive outcome, equal error rates generally cannot be achieved together with scores that mean the same thing in every group (Hardt et al. discuss this result of Kleinberg et al.). Pushing the metric towards 0 can therefore leave a risk score less well calibrated for one group, a trade-off the metric does not weigh.

A score of 0 does not show that the model is fair. The measure uses only predictions, true outcomes and group membership, and Hardt et al. show that situations with very different fairness readings can give identical numbers, so any result needs scrutiny of how the outcome was produced.

Closing the gaps can mean degrading the better-served group instead of improving the other. Hardt et al. show that a predictor meeting equalised odds is only as good as the weakest group's performance, so reaching a score of 0 this way can cost accuracy for everyone.

Results: A total of 298,276 patients aged 40-79 years were included, with an average follow-up time of 8 years (SD=3), of which 9% (N=26,761) self-identified as multiracial. In aggregate, 3.9% of multiracial patients developed ASCVD, ranging from 2.9% (Multiple Asian) to 5.4% (Multiracial American Indian/Alaska Native), compared to 4.4% of all single-race patients. Discriminatory performance of the AHA PREVENT ASCVD Equation was good for aggregated multiracial groups (AUC=0.747), ranging from 0.692 (Multiracial Black) to 0.793 (Multiracial Pacific Islander), and was comparable to single-race groups (AUC=0.753). Calibration was generally good among most multiracial groups. However, the AHA PREVENT ASCVD Equation was fairer in its predictive ability when compared to the PCE for all three fairness metrics. Conclusions and relevance: With good discriminatory ability and calibration for single race and multiracial groups, the AHA PREVENT ASCVD Equation provides both more accurate and fairer estimates of ASCVD risk compared to PCE.

resources.title: Machine learning evaluation of pneumonia severity: subgroup performance in the Medical Imaging and Data Resource Center modified radiographic assessment of lung edema mastermind challenge
resources.abstract: PurposeThe Medical Imaging and Data Resource Center Mastermind Grand Challenge of modified radiographic assessment of lung edema (mRALE) tasked participants with developing machine learning techniques for automated COVID-19 severity assessment via mRALE scores on portable chest radiographs (CXRs). We examine potential biases across demographic subgroups for the best-performing models of the nine teams participating in the test phase of the challenge.ApproachModels were evaluated against a nonpublic test set of CXRs (814 patients) annotated by radiologists for disease severity (mRALE score 0 to 24). Participants used a variety of data and methods for training. Performance was measured using quadratic-weighted kappa (QWK). Bias analyses considered demographics (sex, age, race, ethnicity, and their intersections) using QWK. In addition, for distinguishing no/mild versus moderate/severe disease, equal opportunity difference (EOD) and average absolute odds difference (AAOD) were calculated. Bias was defined as statistically significant QWK subgroup differences, or EOD outside [−0.1; 0.1], or AAOD outside [0; 0.1].ResultsThe nine models demonstrated good agreement with the reference standard (QWK 0.74 to 0.88). The winning model (QWK = 0.884 [0.819; 0.949]) was the only model without biases identified in terms of QWK. The runner-up model (QWK = 0.874 [0.813; 0.936]) showed no identified biases in terms of EOD and AAOD, whereas the winning model disadvantaged three subgroups in each of these metrics. The median number of disadvantaged subgroups for all models was 3.ConclusionsThe challenge demonstrated strong model performances but identified subgroup disparities. Bias analysis is essential as models with similar accuracy may exhibit varying fairness.

techniques.name: Fair Bayesian Optimisation
techniques.description: Fair Bayesian Optimisation (FairBO) tunes a model's hyperparameters, the settings fixed before training such as tree depth or regularisation strength, to find the most accurate model that also meets a fairness threshold chosen in advance, for example a difference in positive-prediction rates between two groups of at most 0.05. Because it only changes hyperparameters and retrains, it treats the model and its training pipeline as a black box, so it works with any model class and any group fairness metric, can enforce several metrics at once, and returns a model that need not use the protected attribute at prediction time (the attribute is still needed to measure fairness during the search). Each step trains a model with a candidate configuration and measures its validation accuracy and fairness, and two Gaussian processes (statistical models that predict a value together with its uncertainty) are fitted to the results of the configurations tried so far. The next configuration is the one with the highest expected improvement in accuracy weighted by the predicted probability of meeting the fairness constraint; until a fair configuration has been found, the search maximises that probability alone. The output is the best configuration that met the constraint, with its accuracy and fairness measurements.

example_use_cases.description: A lender's model risk team tunes a gradient-boosted credit-risk model under a constraint that the approval-rate difference between applicants of different nationality stays at or below 0.05. It records the most accurate configuration that met the constraint beside the result of unconstrained tuning, so the model approval committee can see what accuracy the constraint cost.

An HR analytics team at a large employer tunes a random forest that ranks job applications for interview, enforcing limits on the gender gap in true positive rates and on the gap in shortlisting rates at the same time, because its policy commits to both equal opportunity and comparable shortlisting rates.

A data science team at a health insurer already runs an adversarially debiased claims-triage model whose fairness changed sharply with its learning rate and adversary weight. It uses FairBO to tune those hyperparameters under a statistical parity constraint, rather than tuning them for accuracy alone and checking fairness afterwards.

A local authority building a model to prioritise benefit-fraud reviews cannot use ethnicity as an input at decision time. It holds ethnicity only in a validation extract, uses FairBO to select hyperparameters that keep the referral-rate gap within its equality impact assessment threshold, and then confirms the gap on a separate held-out sample before deployment.

limitations.description: It can only reach fairness that some hyperparameter setting already provides. If no configuration in the search space meets the threshold, it returns no fair model. The originating paper found that regularisation hyperparameters (tree depth, weight penalties, learning rate) have the largest effect on fairness, so a search space without them leaves fewer fair options.

The fairness metric and its threshold must be fixed before the search, and the result says nothing about metrics that were not constrained. Choosing them is a normative decision the method does not make. If decision-makers need to see the whole accuracy-fairness trade-off before picking a threshold, a multi-objective search is needed, which the paper found slower to reach a model meeting a given threshold.

A constraint can be met by a model that barely distinguishes between anyone. The paper argues that as regularisation grows, predictions approach a constant and satisfy every group fairness metric, and in its example run on the Adult dataset (random forest, parity gap at most 0.05) random search found fair models only at the accuracy of always predicting the majority class. Check accuracy and error rates within each group, not only the fairness gap, before accepting the result.

Every step trains a full model, so the cost is the training cost multiplied by the number of evaluations (the paper used up to 100), which is expensive for large models. The fairness value guiding the search is estimated on the validation split used during tuning, so it carries sampling error that is large when a group is small; confirm the gap on held-out data before relying on it.

It has little evidence behind it and no maintained implementation. The paper tests only binary classification with a binary protected attribute on three tabular datasets, leaving regression, image and language tasks to future work. The code shipped in AutoGluon 0.3.1 (2021) and was dropped in 0.4.0; Syne Tune moved it to a legacy folder in 0.14 and removed it in 0.15 (December 2025), though its documentation still describes it. Use means pinning an old release or rebuilding it.

resources.title: Fair Bayesian Optimization
resources.abstract: Given the increasing importance of machine learning (ML) in our lives, several algorithmic fairness techniques have been proposed to mitigate biases in the outcomes of the ML models. However, most of these techniques are specialized to cater to a single family of ML models and a specific definition of fairness, limiting their adaptibility in practice. We introduce a general constrained Bayesian optimization (BO) framework to optimize the performance of any ML model while enforcing one or multiple fairness constraints. BO is a model-agnostic optimization method that has been successfully applied to automatically tune the hyperparameters of ML models. We apply BO with fairness constraints to a range of popular models, including random forests, gradient boosting, and neural networks, showing that we can obtain accurate and fair solutions by acting solely on the hyperparameters. We also show empirically that our approach is competitive with specialized techniques that enforce model-specific fairness constraints, and outperforms preprocessing methods that learn fair representations of the input data. Moreover, our method can be used in synergy with such specialized fairness techniques to tune their hyperparameters. Finally, we study the relationship between fairness and the hyperparameters selected by BO. We observe a correlation between regularization and unbiased models, explaining why acting on the hyperparameters leads to ML models that generalize well and are fair.

techniques.name: Adversarial Training Evaluation
techniques.description: Adversarial training evaluation tests whether a model trained on adversarial examples (inputs altered slightly to cause errors) is really more robust, or has only learned to resist the attacks used in training. The evaluator first states a threat model, meaning the kind and size of change allowed and what the attacker knows. The model is then attacked with a varied set of strong methods, including ones not used in training, ones adapted to this particular defence, and ones that do not rely on the model's gradients, which exposes models that merely hide them. The main output is robust accuracy, the share of inputs still classified correctly under attack, plotted against the allowed size of the change and reported next to accuracy on unaltered inputs. Because attacks can only find weaknesses, the result is an upper bound on robustness, not a guarantee.

example_use_cases.description: A building-access provider trains its face-recognition model with adversarial examples from a single standard attack. Before relying on it, the security team attacks the model with methods not used in training, including a gradient-free attack, and reports robust accuracy at the perturbation size in its threat model, to check the gain is not overfitting to the training attack.

A mail provider adversarially trains its spam filter against text-perturbation attacks. The evaluation measures how much attacker-altered spam still gets through when attacks not used in training are applied, and how the false-positive rate on ordinary mail has changed, to decide whether the clean-accuracy cost of the hardened filter is acceptable.

A hospital adversarially trains a tumour-detection classifier for scans. The evaluation attacks it with a strong attack ensemble at several perturbation sizes and compares accuracy on routine scans before and after hardening, to decide whether the hardened model is safe to deploy in the screening workflow.

A driver-assistance supplier trains its road-sign classifier against changes of up to a fixed size per pixel. The evaluation also attacks it with a different kind of change (a limit on total distortion across the image) and with rotations and shifts, to see whether the robustness holds outside the threat model used in training.

limitations.description: The result is an upper bound on robustness, not a guarantee. Robust accuracy is measured against the attacks that were run, so a model that survives them can still be broken by a stronger attack, and an evaluation can never prove that no attack exists.

Findings hold only for the threat model tested. Robustness to changes of one kind and size says little about other kinds or larger sizes, so each result must be reported with the perturbation type, size and attacker knowledge it assumed.

Weak or poorly tuned attacks overstate robustness. Default settings, a single attack or the attack used in training can leave a model looking robust, and gradient masking can make gradient-based attacks fail. In one large study, a standard attack ensemble lowered the robust accuracy reported for 13 of over 50 published models by more than 10%.

A thorough evaluation is expensive and needs expertise. Strong attacks run many iterations and restarts, gradient-free and hard-label attacks need far more queries, and attacks often have to be adapted to the defence by someone who understands how it works.

Attack methods keep improving, so a result is dated. The evaluation should be repeated when stronger attacks appear and should include attacks not used in training or tuning, which means keeping a current set of attack methods.

resources.title: On Evaluating Adversarial Robustness
resources.abstract: Correctly evaluating defenses against adversarial examples has proven to be extremely difficult. Despite the significant amount of recent work attempting to design defenses that withstand adaptive attacks, few have succeeded; most papers that propose defenses are quickly shown to be incorrect. We believe a large contributing factor is the difficulty of performing security evaluations. In this paper, we discuss the methodological foundations, review commonly accepted best practices, and suggest new methods for evaluating defenses to adversarial examples. We hope that both researchers developing defenses as well as readers and reviewers who wish to understand the completeness of an evaluation consider our advice in order to avoid common pitfalls.

resources.title: Reliable evaluation of adversarial robustness with an ensemble of diverse parameter-free attacks
resources.abstract: The field of defense strategies against adversarial attacks has significantly grown over the last years, but progress is hampered as the evaluation of adversarial defenses is often insufficient and thus gives a wrong impression of robustness. Many promising defenses could be broken later on, making it difficult to identify the state-of-the-art. Frequent pitfalls in the evaluation are improper tuning of hyperparameters of the attacks, gradient obfuscation or masking. In this paper we first propose two extensions of the PGD-attack overcoming failures due to suboptimal step size and problems of the objective function. We then combine our novel attacks with two complementary existing ones to form a parameter-free, computationally affordable and user-independent ensemble of attacks to test adversarial robustness. We apply our ensemble to over 50 models from papers published at recent top machine learning and computer vision venues. In all except one of the cases we achieve lower robust test accuracy than reported in these papers, often by more than $10\%$, identifying several broken defenses.

Learning Interpretable Features via Adversarially Robust Optimization
resources.abstract: Neural networks are proven to be remarkably successful for classification and diagnosis in medical applications. However, the ambiguity in the decision-making process and the interpretability of the learned features is a matter of concern. In this work, we propose a method for improving the feature interpretability of neural network classifiers. Initially, we propose a baseline convolutional neural network with state of the art performance in terms of accuracy and weakly supervised localization. Subsequently, the loss is modified to integrate robustness to adversarial examples into the training process. In this work, feature interpretability is quantified via evaluating the weakly supervised localization using the ground truth bounding boxes. Interpretability is also visually assessed using class activation maps and saliency maps. The method is applied to NIH ChestX-ray14, the largest publicly available chest x-rays dataset. We demonstrate that the adversarially robust optimization paradigm improves feature interpretability both quantitatively and visually.

techniques.name: Chain-of-Thought Faithfulness Evaluation
techniques.description: Chain-of-thought faithfulness evaluation tests whether the step-by-step reasoning a language model writes out is what actually produces its answer, rather than an account added afterwards. One set of tests alters the reasoning itself, by cutting it short, inserting a deliberate mistake, rewording it or replacing it with filler text, and checks whether the final answer changes. If the answer never changes, the reasoning is probably not doing the work. Another set adds a cue to the input that points to a particular answer, such as a user's stated guess, and checks whether the answer shifts while the explanation never mentions the cue. Each test gives a rate, such as how often the answer changes, and passing one rules out a single kind of unfaithfulness without showing that the reasoning is faithful or that its steps are correct.

example_use_cases.description: An education company's tutoring assistant shows pupils its step-by-step working beside each answer to a science question. Before telling pupils that the working explains the answer, the evaluation team cuts the working short and inserts a deliberate mistake on a test set, and records how often the final answer changes. Where it rarely does, as Lanham et al. found for grade-school science sets, the working is shown as an illustration, not as the reason.

A lender's model-validation team lets an underwriting assistant write a rationale for each recommendation that staff keep on file. It reruns validation cases with a line added saying a senior colleague favours approval. Where the recommendation moves towards the line but the rationale never mentions it, as Turpin et al. found for suggested answers, the rationale is not accepted as the record of why the case was decided.

A public body choosing between two sizes of one language-model family for a casework summarising tool wants staff to rely on the reasoning the model shows. On multiple-choice questions built from its own case files, it records how often each model's answer changes when its reasoning is removed, shuffling answer order to control for letter preference as Bentham et al. did, and prefers the model whose answers depend on its reasoning.

A recruitment platform's audit team uses a language model to compare two candidates for shortlisting when the evidence for each is thin. Following the social-bias test in Turpin et al., it submits each pair twice with the weak evidence swapped between the candidates and counts pairs where the same candidate is picked both times. Those pairs show evidence weighed inconsistently, so the reasoning is not accepted as showing what drove the choice.

limitations.description: Passing does not show faithfulness. Each test rules out one way the reasoning could be unfaithful, and the authors call the tests necessary but not sufficient. There is no independent view of the model's actual process to check against, so a clean result supports a narrower claim than 'the reasoning is faithful'.

Results do not carry over between models or tasks. Lanham et al. found that the reasoning changed the final answer under 10% of the time on three science question sets but over 60% on algebra word problems, and that faithfulness varied with model size. Re-measure for the model version and task type that will be deployed.

The answer-change score can reflect something other than faithfulness. Bentham et al. repeated Lanham et al.'s measure on three other model families. After correcting for a model's habit of favouring certain answer letters, apparent unfaithfulness in weaker models fell sharply, and the corrected score tracked accuracy (R-squared of 0.74).

Input-cue tests find only the influences the evaluator thinks to add. Turpin et al. tried three cues, and say their setup only tests faithfulness against minor changes to the input. A model that passes can still be swayed by a cue nobody tried, and the cue must point to a wrong answer to show up as an accuracy drop.

The tests are costly and need control of generation. Lanham et al. sampled 100 reasoning chains per question and re-queried after each truncation; Turpin et al. subsampled for cost. Inserted mistakes were judged plausible in at least 80% of cases, so up to a fifth may test nothing, and Bentham et al. note the procedure needs manual intervention in decoding.

resources.title: cot-unfaithfulness (code for Turpin et al. 2023)
Language Models Don't Always Say What They Think: Unfaithful Explanations in Chain-of-Thought Prompting
resources.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) can achieve strong performance on many tasks by producing step-by-step reasoning before giving a final output, often referred to as chain-of-thought reasoning (CoT). It is tempting to interpret these CoT explanations as the LLM's process for solving a task. This level of transparency into LLMs' predictions would yield significant safety benefits. However, we find that CoT explanations can systematically misrepresent the true reason for a model's prediction. We demonstrate that CoT explanations can be heavily influenced by adding biasing features to model inputs--e.g., by reordering the multiple-choice options in a few-shot prompt to make the answer always "(A)"--which models systematically fail to mention in their explanations. When we bias models toward incorrect answers, they frequently generate CoT explanations rationalizing those answers. This causes accuracy to drop by as much as 36% on a suite of 13 tasks from BIG-Bench Hard, when testing with GPT-3.5 from OpenAI and Claude 1.0 from Anthropic. On a social-bias task, model explanations justify giving answers in line with stereotypes without mentioning the influence of these social biases. Our findings indicate that CoT explanations can be plausible yet misleading, which risks increasing our trust in LLMs without guaranteeing their safety. Building more transparent and explainable systems will require either improving CoT faithfulness through targeted efforts or abandoning CoT in favor of alternative methods.

resources.title: Measuring Faithfulness in Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
resources.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) perform better when they produce step-by-step, "Chain-of-Thought" (CoT) reasoning before answering a question, but it is unclear if the stated reasoning is a faithful explanation of the model's actual reasoning (i.e., its process for answering the question). We investigate hypotheses for how CoT reasoning may be unfaithful, by examining how the model predictions change when we intervene on the CoT (e.g., by adding mistakes or paraphrasing it). Models show large variation across tasks in how strongly they condition on the CoT when predicting their answer, sometimes relying heavily on the CoT and other times primarily ignoring it. CoT's performance boost does not seem to come from CoT's added test-time compute alone or from information encoded via the particular phrasing of the CoT. As models become larger and more capable, they produce less faithful reasoning on most tasks we study. Overall, our results suggest that CoT can be faithful if the circumstances such as the model size and task are carefully chosen.

resources.title: Chain-of-Thought Unfaithfulness as Disguised Accuracy
resources.abstract: Understanding the extent to which Chain-of-Thought (CoT) generations align with a large language model's (LLM) internal computations is critical for deciding whether to trust an LLM's output. As a proxy for CoT faithfulness, Lanham et al. (2023) propose a metric that measures a model's dependence on its CoT for producing an answer. Within a single family of proprietary models, they find that LLMs exhibit a scaling-then-inverse-scaling relationship between model size and their measure of faithfulness, and that a 13 billion parameter model exhibits increased faithfulness compared to models ranging from 810 million to 175 billion parameters in size. We evaluate whether these results generalize as a property of all LLMs. We replicate the experimental setup in their section focused on scaling experiments with three different families of models and, under specific conditions, successfully reproduce the scaling trends for CoT faithfulness they report. However, after normalizing the metric to account for a model's bias toward certain answer choices, unfaithfulness drops significantly for smaller less-capable models. This normalized faithfulness metric is also strongly correlated ($R^2$=0.74) with accuracy, raising doubts about its validity for evaluating faithfulness.

techniques.name: Constitutional AI Evaluation
techniques.description: Constitutional AI evaluation checks whether a language model follows the written principles, or 'constitution', that it was trained or instructed to follow. The evaluator writes test prompts for each principle, and can add prompts where two principles conflict or where a user tries to talk the model out of a principle. A judge, either human reviewers or a second language model whose accuracy has been checked, assesses each response against one principle at a time, often by comparing it with a baseline model's response. The result is a rate for each principle, such as how often the model's response is preferred to the baseline's, which shows which principles it follows well on the prompts tested and which it does not. A fuller evaluation also checks that following the principles has not made the model over-cautious or less capable.

example_use_cases.description: A developer tuning a general-purpose assistant on a constitution that includes 'refuse requests for illegal activity' writes test prompts for each principle, including borderline chemistry-education questions and attempts to extract synthesis instructions. Reviewers compare the tuned model's answers with the base model's, to decide whether the constitution is ready to ship or needs principles rewritten.

A news publisher using an AI summariser governed by a neutrality principle gives it the same contested story framed from several political positions. Reviewers from differing viewpoints score whether each summary adds editorial language, and the editors use the rate by topic to decide where the summariser can run without a human check.

A digital health provider tests a mental health support chatbot built on the principle 'be supportive, but never diagnose' with scripted crisis conversations in which users ask directly for a diagnosis. Clinicians score each reply, and the share that stays on the right side of the boundary decides whether the chatbot is cleared for a limited pilot.

An education company checks a homework assistant built on the principle 'guide learning without giving direct answers' across subjects, age bands and frustrated or urgent requests. It counts replies that simply give the answer, and uses the rate for each subject to decide where the principle needs strengthening before a school rollout.

limitations.description: Principles are written in natural language, so compliance depends on how the judge reads them. Vague principles, or ones that mean different things across cultures and languages, give scores that reviewers would dispute, so the judge's reading needs checking against human reviewers for each principle.

Principles can conflict in complex scenarios, and the evaluation has to decide which should win. If the intended priority is not written down, a model can look compliant on each principle separately and still resolve conflicts differently from what the developer intended.

Adherence is uneven across kinds of principle. In one study of small fine-tuned models, negatively framed principles such as avoiding harmful content were followed much better than positively framed, abstract ones such as benefiting humanity, so an average score can hide principles the model largely ignores.

Scores depend on the test prompts and on the judge. Prompts that miss a principle's edge cases give a falsely high rate, and an automated judge can favour one response position or misapply the principle, so it needs checking against human judgement in each new domain.

When principles are revised after deployment, results must be re-run, and comparing them across principle versions is hard because a change in score may come from the model, the principles or the test criteria.

resources.title: C3AI: Crafting and Evaluating Constitutions for Constitutional AI
resources.abstract: Constitutional AI (CAI) guides LLM behavior using constitutions, but identifying which principles are most effective for model alignment remains an open challenge. We introduce the C3AI framework (Crafting Constitutions for CAI models), which serves two key functions: (1) selecting and structuring principles to form effective constitutions before fine-tuning; and (2) evaluating whether fine-tuned CAI models follow these principles in practice. By analyzing principles from AI and psychology, we found that positively framed, behavior-based principles align more closely with human preferences than negatively framed or trait-based principles. In a safety alignment use case, we applied a graph-based principle selection method to refine an existing CAI constitution, improving safety measures while maintaining strong general reasoning capabilities. Interestingly, fine-tuned CAI models performed well on negatively framed principles but struggled with positively framed ones, in contrast to our human alignment results. This highlights a potential gap between principle design and model adherence. Overall, C3AI provides a structured and scalable approach to both crafting and evaluating CAI constitutions.

resources.title: Constitutional AI: Harmlessness from AI Feedback
resources.abstract: As AI systems become more capable, we would like to enlist their help to supervise other AIs. We experiment with methods for training a harmless AI assistant through self-improvement, without any human labels identifying harmful outputs. The only human oversight is provided through a list of rules or principles, and so we refer to the method as 'Constitutional AI'. The process involves both a supervised learning and a reinforcement learning phase. In the supervised phase we sample from an initial model, then generate self-critiques and revisions, and then finetune the original model on revised responses. In the RL phase, we sample from the finetuned model, use a model to evaluate which of the two samples is better, and then train a preference model from this dataset of AI preferences. We then train with RL using the preference model as the reward signal, i.e. we use 'RL from AI Feedback' (RLAIF). As a result we are able to train a harmless but non-evasive AI assistant that engages with harmful queries by explaining its objections to them. Both the SL and RL methods can leverage chain-of-thought style reasoning to improve the human-judged performance and transparency of AI decision making. These methods make it possible to control AI behavior more precisely and with far fewer human labels.

resources.title: Domain-Specific Constitutional AI: Enhancing Safety in LLM-Powered Mental Health Chatbots
resources.abstract: Mental health applications have emerged as a critical area in computational health, driven by rising global rates of mental illness, the integration of AI in psychological care, and the need for scalable solutions in underserved communities. These include therapy chatbots, crisis detection, and wellness platforms handling sensitive data, requiring specialized AI safety beyond general safeguards due to emotional vulnerability, risks like misdiagnosis or symptom exacerbation, and precise management of vulnerable states to avoid severe outcomes such as self-harm or loss of trust. Despite AI safety advances, general safeguards inadequately address mental health-specific challenges, including crisis intervention accuracy to avert escalations, therapeutic guideline adherence to prevent misinformation, scale limitations in resource-constrained settings, and adaptation to nuanced dialogues where generics may introduce biases or miss distress signals. We introduce an approach to apply Constitutional AI training with domain-specific mental health principles for safe, domain-adapted CAI systems in computational mental health applications.

resources.title: Collective Constitutional AI: Aligning a Language Model with Public Input
resources.abstract: There is growing consensus that language model (LM) developers should not be the sole deciders of LM behavior, creating a need for methods that enable the broader public to collectively shape the behavior of LM systems that affect them. To address this need, we present Collective Constitutional AI (CCAI): a multi-stage process for sourcing and integrating public input into LMs—from identifying a target population to sourcing principles to training and evaluating a model. We demonstrate the real-world practicality of this approach by creating what is, to our knowledge, the first LM fine-tuned with collectively sourced public input and evaluating this model against a baseline model trained with established principles from a LM developer. Our quantitative evaluations demonstrate several benefits of our approach: the CCAI-trained model shows lower bias across nine social dimensions compared to the baseline model, while maintaining equivalent performance on language, math, and helpful-harmless evaluations. Qualitative comparisons of the models suggest that the models differ on the basis of their respective constitutions, e.g., when prompted with contentious topics, the CCAI-trained model tends to generate responses that reframe the matter positively instead of a refusal. These results demonstrate a promising, tractable pathway toward publicly informed development of language models.

techniques.name: Continual Learning Stability Testing
techniques.description: Continual learning stability testing checks whether a model that is updated over time with new data or tasks keeps what it learned earlier, by scoring it after each update on a test set for every task in the sequence. Backward transfer is the average change in accuracy on earlier tasks, and a large fall is called catastrophic forgetting. Forward transfer is accuracy on a task the model has not yet been trained on, compared with an untrained model. Scoring only at the end of each update can hide a sharp but temporary drop, so stricter tests also score the model during training and report its worst result. The scores can also show whether methods meant to protect old knowledge, such as replaying stored examples of earlier data or penalising changes to the weights that matter for earlier tasks, are working.

example_use_cases.description: A trust-and-safety team retrains its abuse classifier every month on newly reported content. Before release it scores the new version on a held-out test set for each earlier abuse type and holds the release if detection of any type has fallen by more than the agreed margin.

A hospital team lets a triage model keep learning from new cases while it is in use. Because users meet any dip as it happens, the team scores the model on its urgent conditions at regular points during each update, not only at the end, and stops the update if the lowest score falls below the agreed floor.

A bank updates its fraud model weekly on newly confirmed cases. To see whether replaying stored examples of older fraud actually protects detection of old patterns, the team runs the same update with and without replay and compares how well each version still catches each earlier fraud type.

A factory retrains a camera-based hazard detector when a new machine is installed. Before it returns to the line, the safety engineer scores the retrained detector on the stored test images for every previously known hazard and signs off only if none is detected less reliably than before.

limitations.description: Every update means scoring the model on a test set for each earlier task, so total cost grows with the number of tasks as well as the number of updates. Old test sets also have to be kept, which can conflict with data-retention rules, and scoring only a sample of tasks cannot detect forgetting in the rest.

Scores taken only at the end of each update can miss a sharp, temporary drop on earlier tasks while the model is still learning. This matters for a system that stays in service during training, because users meet the dip. Catching it needs repeated scoring during training, which adds to the cost.

Stability scores measure only one side of the stability-plasticity trade-off. A model can score perfectly on earlier tasks by refusing to learn anything new, so results must be read alongside accuracy on the new tasks.

Deciding how much forgetting is acceptable depends on the application, and the test cannot settle it. A threshold set too tight blocks adaptation to changing conditions, and one set too loose lets real losses through.

Results hold for the sequence of tasks tested, and assume tasks with clear boundaries and a labelled test set for each. Real data streams often drift gradually, and how much a model forgets depends on how different consecutive tasks are, so a gentler test sequence understates forgetting.

resources.title: Continual evaluation for lifelong learning: Identifying the stability gap
resources.abstract: Time-dependent data-generating distributions have proven to be difficult for gradient-based training of neural networks, as the greedy updates result in catastrophic forgetting of previously learned knowledge. Despite the progress in the field of continual learning to overcome this forgetting, we show that a set of common state-of-the-art methods still suffers from substantial forgetting upon starting to learn new tasks, except that this forgetting is temporary and followed by a phase of performance recovery. We refer to this intriguing but potentially problematic phenomenon as the stability gap. The stability gap had likely remained under the radar due to standard practice in the field of evaluating continual learning models only after each task. Instead, we establish a framework for continual evaluation that uses per-iteration evaluation and we define a new set of metrics to quantify worst-case performance. Empirically we show that experience replay, constraint-based replay, knowledge-distillation, and parameter regularization methods are all prone to the stability gap; and that the stability gap can be observed in class-, task-, and domain-incremental learning benchmarks. Additionally, a controlled experiment shows that the stability gap increases when tasks are more dissimilar. Finally, by disentangling gradients into plasticity and stability components, we propose a conceptual explanation for the stability gap.

resources.title: Gradient Episodic Memory for Continual Learning
resources.abstract: One major obstacle towards AI is the poor ability of models to solve new problems quicker, and without forgetting previously acquired knowledge. To better understand this issue, we study the problem of continual learning, where the model observes, once and one by one, examples concerning a sequence of tasks. First, we propose a set of metrics to evaluate models learning over a continuum of data. These metrics characterize models not only by their test accuracy, but also in terms of their ability to transfer knowledge across tasks. Second, we propose a model for continual learning, called Gradient Episodic Memory (GEM) that alleviates forgetting, while allowing beneficial transfer of knowledge to previous tasks. Our experiments on variants of the MNIST and CIFAR-100 datasets demonstrate the strong performance of GEM when compared to the state-of-the-art.

resources.title: Development and validation of deep continual learning model to sequentially learn multiple clinical prediction tasks for ICU patients
resources.abstract: BACKGROUND ICU patients often suffer from critical and complex condition, and multiple potential risks should be monitored to provide them comprehensive care. However, no study proposes continual learning (CL) model that can effectively solve multiple clinical prediction tasks without catastrophic forgetting. This study proposes three deep CL models for ICU patients. METHODS Three public ICU databases were employed. The included patients from MIMIC-III and MIMIC-IV were divided into eight task sets, and the patients from eICU-CRD composed the test set. We propose three CL models (CL_1, CL_2, CL_3) to sequentially learn eight prediction tasks on the eight task sets, and then externally validate them on the test set. We compare our models to three representative baseline CL models and the single-task (ST) and multi-task (MT) model. We train all the CL models under different orders, and evaluate their prediction performance by multiple metrics and their memory ability by backward transfer (BWT). We also analyzed the effect of previously learned tasks on learning new tasks. RESULTS Our three CL models had comparable or slightly weaker performance compared to ST and MT model on the eight tasks. They effectively mitigated catastrophic forgetting, and their performance is robust to different training orders. CL_2 and CL_3 even have improved performance on the current task after learning some previous tasks. Our three CL models outperformed the baseline CL models in most experiments. CONCLUSIONS Our CL models are promising to sequentially learn multiple clinical prediction tasks for ICU patients. The CL_2 and CL_3 show the ability of utilizing information of previous tasks to improve learning new tasks. More new datasets and tasks are still needed to further verify the validity of the CL models.

techniques.name: Few-Shot Fairness Evaluation
techniques.description: Few-shot fairness evaluation tests whether the worked examples placed in a prompt change how fairly a language model treats different demographic groups. The evaluator builds many versions of the same prompt, varying which examples appear and how each demographic group is represented among them. Each version is run on the same test inputs, and group-level results are compared across versions. Typical checks include the gap in outcomes between groups, whether outputs echo stereotypes present in the examples, and whether an input gets the same treatment when only a demographic term in it is swapped. The result shows how sensitive the model's fairness is to the choice of examples, and which compositions make outcomes more or less even.

example_use_cases.description: Testing whether a resume screening LLM's few-shot examples inadvertently introduce gender bias by showing more male examples for technical positions, affecting how it evaluates subsequent applicants.

Evaluating whether a medical triage LLM's few-shot examples for symptom assessment inadvertently encode demographic biases (e.g., more examples of cardiac symptoms in male patients), leading to differential urgency assessments across patient populations.

Assessing whether few-shot examples in a loan application review assistant systematically present more favourable examples for certain demographic profiles, biasing the model's assessment of creditworthiness for subsequent applications.

Testing whether an automated essay grading system keeps consistent standards across student demographics when its few-shot examples over-represent particular writing styles, dialects or cultural references.

limitations.description: The number of possible example sets, orderings and wordings is far too large to test exhaustively. The evaluation samples configurations and can miss the combinations that cause the worst disparities, so results describe what was tested rather than every prompt the system will meet.

Fairness measures can shift with small changes in example wording, order or prompt format, and with ordinary sampling variation in the model's replies. A gap between two example sets may be noise unless each is run repeatedly, and results seldom carry over to a different prompt template, instruction style or model version.

Needs test inputs labelled with demographic attributes, or pairs of inputs that differ only in a demographic term. These can be unavailable, costly to build or sensitive to hold, and they must reflect how the system will actually be prompted, which takes domain expertise to judge.

Each extra example set multiplies the number of model calls, because every set must be run on enough inputs for each group being compared. With large models and high inference costs, thorough coverage is expensive, which tempts teams to test fewer configurations.

resources.title: Fairness-guided few-shot prompting for large language models
resources.abstract: Large language models have demonstrated surprising ability to perform in-context learning, i.e., these models can be directly applied to solve numerous downstream tasks by conditioning on a prompt constructed by a few input-output examples. However, prior research has shown that in-context learning can suffer from high instability due to variations in training examples, example order, and prompt formats. Therefore, the construction of an appropriate prompt is essential for improving the performance of in-context learning. In this paper, we revisit this problem from the view of predictive bias. Specifically, we introduce a metric to evaluate the predictive bias of a fixed prompt against labels or a given attributes. Then we empirically show that prompts with higher bias always lead to unsatisfactory predictive quality. Based on this observation, we propose a novel search strategy based on the greedy search to identify the near-optimal prompt for improving the performance of in-context learning. We perform comprehensive experiments with state-of-the-art mainstream models such as GPT-3 on various downstream tasks. Our results indicate that our method can enhance the model's in-context learning performance in an effective and interpretable manner.

resources.title: Strategic Demonstration Selection for Improved Fairness in LLM In-Context Learning
resources.abstract: Recent studies highlight the effectiveness of using in-context learning (ICL) to steer large language models (LLMs) in processing tabular data, a challenging task given the structured nature of such data.Despite advancements in performance, the fairness implications of these methods are less understood.This study investigates how varying demonstrations within ICL prompts influence the fairness outcomes of LLMs.Our findings reveal that deliberately including minority group samples in prompts significantly boosts fairness without sacrificing predictive accuracy.Further experiments demonstrate that the proportion of minority to majority samples in demonstrations affects the trade-off between fairness and prediction accuracy.Based on these insights, we introduce a mitigation technique that employs clustering and evolutionary strategies to curate a diverse and representative sample set from the training data.This approach aims to enhance both predictive performance and fairness in ICL applications.Experimental results validate that our proposed method dramatically improves fairness across various metrics, showing its efficacy in real-world scenarios.

techniques.name: Knowledge Boundary Probing
techniques.description: Knowledge boundary probing maps what a language model can and cannot reliably answer. A probe set is built from questions across the topics the system will face, including some with known answers and some that cannot be answered. Each question is asked in several phrasings, because a model may answer one wording correctly and fail on another. Responses are scored for correctness, for whether the model signals doubt when it should, and for whether its stated or computed confidence tracks whether it is right. The result is a topic-by-topic map of what the model knows, knows only under some phrasings, and does not know, which informs where to deploy it, what to tell users about its limits, and where to add training data or human review.

example_use_cases.description: A government analytics team using an LLM to summarise policy evidence probes it on well-researched areas and on recent or local policy it cannot have seen in training. Accuracy drops on the second group, so the team adds a retrieval step for those topics before the tool is used in briefings.

A bank adds a per-topic table of probe results (accurate on card fees, weak on mortgage rules) to the model documentation for its customer-service chatbot. The app uses the table to tell customers when to check with an adviser.

A school-software vendor checks an LLM maths tutor against each curriculum unit, asking every question in several wordings. Units where correctness changes with the wording are marked for teacher review instead of being shown to students unsupervised.

limitations.description: The probe set samples a finite number of topics and question types. A clean result on those says little about topics the set omits, so the map is only as broad as the probes, and mapping every domain is infeasible.

Whether a model 'knows' something depends on how the question is worded. A single phrasing can understate or overstate what the model knows, so each question needs several phrasings, and the boundary is fuzzy rather than a clean line.

Models can be confidently wrong, and can hedge on things they know, so stated or computed confidence is only a rough guide to knowledge. Calibration also varies by topic, so one overall score can hide weak areas.

Scoring needs labelled questions and a way to detect hedging. Deciding which questions are truly unanswerable takes human judgement, and detectors built on one model's uncertainty phrases may miss how other models express doubt.
The map holds for one model version. Fine-tuning, a model update or added retrieval shifts the boundary, so the probes must be rerun after each change to keep the map accurate.

Benchmarking Knowledge Boundary for Large Language Models: A Different Perspective on Model Evaluation
resources.abstract: In recent years, substantial advancements have been made in the development of large language models, achieving remarkable performance across diverse tasks. To evaluate the knowledge ability of language models, previous studies have proposed lots of benchmarks based on question-answering pairs. We argue that it is not reliable and comprehensive to evaluate language models with a fixed question or limited paraphrases as the query, since language models are sensitive to prompt. Therefore, we introduce a novel concept named knowledge boundary to encompass both prompt-agnostic and prompt-sensitive knowledge within language models. Knowledge boundary avoids prompt sensitivity in language model evaluations, rendering them more dependable and robust. To explore the knowledge boundary for a given model, we propose projected gradient descent method with semantic constraints, a new algorithm designed to identify the optimal prompt for each piece of knowledge. Experiments demonstrate a superior performance of our algorithm in computing the knowledge boundary compared to existing methods. Furthermore, we evaluate the ability of multiple language models in several domains with knowledge boundary.

resources.title: Do Large Language Models Know What They Don’t Know?
resources.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have a wealth of knowledge that allows them to excel in various Natural Language Processing (NLP) tasks.Current research focuses on enhancing their performance within their existing knowledge.Despite their vast knowledge, LLMs are still limited by the amount of information they can accommodate and comprehend.Therefore, the ability to understand their own limitations on the unknows, referred to as self-knowledge, is of paramount importance.This study aims to evaluate LLMs' self-knowledge by assessing their ability to identify unanswerable or unknowable questions.We introduce an automated methodology to detect uncertainty in the responses of these models, providing a novel measure of their self-knowledge.We further introduce a unique dataset, SelfAware, consisting of unanswerable questions from five diverse categories and their answerable counterparts.Our extensive analysis, involving 20 LLMs including GPT-3, InstructGPT, and LLaMA, discovering an intrinsic capacity for self-knowledge within these models.Moreover, we demonstrate that in-context learning and instruction tuning can further enhance this self-knowledge.Despite this promising insight, our findings also highlight a considerable gap between the capabilities of these models and human proficiency in recognizing the limits of their knowledge. "True wisdom is knowing what you don't know." -Confucius

resources.title: Aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty in machine learning: an introduction to concepts and methods
resources.abstract: The notion of uncertainty is of major importance in machine learning and constitutes a key element of machine learning methodology. In line with the statistical tradition, uncertainty has long been perceived as almost synonymous with standard probability and probabilistic predictions. Yet, due to the steadily increasing relevance of machine learning for practical applications and related issues such as safety requirements, new problems and challenges have recently been identified by machine learning scholars, and these problems may call for new methodological developments. In particular, this includes the importance of distinguishing between (at least) two different types of uncertainty, often referred to as aleatoric and epistemic . In this paper, we provide an introduction to the topic of uncertainty in machine learning as well as an overview of attempts so far at handling uncertainty in general and formalizing this distinction in particular.

Calibration of Self-Reported Confidence and Accuracy of Large Language Models in Medical Question Answering
resources.abstract: Objective: To evaluate the alignment between self-reported confidence of large language models (LLM) and their accuracy in answering medical multiple-choice questions. Materials and Methods: We prompted six LLMs (GPT-5, GPT-5-mini, GPT-5-nano, GPT-4o, Claude Sonnet 4.5, and Gemini 2.5) to answer MedMCQA items and report confidence scores. Based on 12,000 LLM responses, we calculated Expected Calibration Errors (ECE) by averaging absolute differences between observed accuracy and predicted confidence. Results: Mean ECE differed by model (Claude Sonnet 4.5 best: 0.06; Gpt-4o worst: 0.127) and varied across specialties (“Skin” best: 0.041; “Social & Preventive Medicine” worst: 0.141). Accuracy of examined LLMs showed analogous variation between specialties. Discussion: Our results demonstrate that high accuracy does not guarantee reliable uncertainty estimation. We identified substantial heterogeneity across medical specialties, where pooled metrics masked a threefold ECE increase between best- and worst-performing domains. Conclusion: We recommend incorporating calibration reporting into LLM evaluations, as larger models exhibit improved “self-knowledge”, but uneven overconfidence persists.

techniques.name: Out-of-Domain Detection
techniques.description: Out-of-domain detection checks whether a user's query falls inside the topics and tasks a conversational AI system is meant to handle. Scope is defined by examples, such as an assistant's supported intents (the actions it can recognise), and a detector then scores how closely each new query resembles them. Typical detectors set a minimum confidence on an intent classifier, add an explicit out-of-scope class trained on examples of unsupported queries, or measure how far a query's embedding, a numerical summary of its meaning, lies from the in-scope examples. A query judged out of scope can be declined, handed to a person or another service, or answered with a request to rephrase, instead of receiving an unreliable or invented answer. The detector tests resemblance to the defined scope, not what the system actually knows, so it needs evaluating on realistic out-of-scope queries.

example_use_cases.description: Enabling a medical chatbot specialised in diabetes management to recognise and deflect questions about unrelated conditions, avoiding potentially dangerous medical advice outside its training domain.

Ensuring an educational AI tutor for high school mathematics reliably identifies advanced university-level questions and redirects students to appropriate resources rather than attempting explanations beyond its scope.

An insurer's claims-intake assistant is built for routine motor and household claims. Messages about unfamiliar claim types, such as large flood events or commercial losses, are detected and routed to a specialist adjuster instead of being handled with irrelevant questions.

A council's resident-services chatbot covers bin collections, parking permits and council tax. When a resident asks about something it does not cover, such as a planning dispute, it says so, names the service that can help and logs the query, and the log shows the council which topics residents ask about that the chatbot cannot answer.

limitations.description: Scope has to be defined before it can be detected, and general-purpose assistants or fuzzy domains have no clean edge. A narrow definition refuses legitimate queries, and a loose one lets unsupported queries through.

Detection is weakest on queries that resemble in-scope ones. In the 2019 benchmark that introduced the task, no intent classifier caught more than about two-thirds of out-of-scope queries even when trained on examples of them, so recall should be measured on realistic out-of-scope queries before the detector is relied on.
The threshold trades wrongly refusing valid queries against wrongly answering unsupported ones. The two errors rarely cost the same, and queries near the boundary will still land on both sides.
Users can rephrase or disguise an unsupported request so that it resembles in-scope wording. A detector tested only on plain phrasings overstates how well it holds up against paraphrase.

Scope changes as capabilities are added or retired, so the detector and its out-of-scope test set need refreshing, or it will refuse newly supported queries and accept newly unsupported ones. Building realistic out-of-scope examples is costly because annotators need expert knowledge of the in-scope intents.

resources.title: An Evaluation Dataset for Intent Classification and Out-of-Scope Prediction
resources.abstract: Task-oriented dialog systems need to know when a query falls outside their range of supported intents, but current text classification corpora only define label sets that cover every example. We introduce a new dataset that includes queries that are out-of-scope—i.e., queries that do not fall into any of the system’s supported intents. This poses a new challenge because models cannot assume that every query at inference time belongs to a system-supported intent class. Our dataset also covers 150 intent classes over 10 domains, capturing the breadth that a production task-oriented agent must handle. We evaluate a range of benchmark classifiers on our dataset along with several different out-of-scope identification schemes. We find that while the classifiers perform well on in-scope intent classification, they struggle to identify out-of-scope queries. Our dataset and evaluation fill an important gap in the field, offering a way of more rigorously and realistically benchmarking text classification in task-driven dialog systems.

techniques.name: Retrieval-Augmented Generation Evaluation
techniques.description: A retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system answers a question by retrieving passages from a document collection and asking a language model to write an answer from them. RAG evaluation scores retrieval on whether the fetched passages are relevant and focused and, where reference answers exist, whether they contain what the answer needs. Generation is scored on faithfulness, usually by splitting the answer into individual claims and reporting the share that the fetched passages support, and on answer relevance, which asks whether the answer addresses the question. Frameworks such as Ragas automate these checks with a second language model acting as judge, so faithfulness and relevance need no human-written reference answers. Test sets can also include questions the documents cannot answer, to check that the system says so instead of guessing.

example_use_cases.description: A software company's support team tests its troubleshooting assistant on a set of real customer questions. For each answer it checks that the retrieved pages are the right ones and that every configuration step or command quoted appears in the official documentation, and it holds back changes that introduce invented steps.

A law firm's research team tests an assistant that summarises case law from its own database. Each summary is split into claims and each claim is checked against the passages the assistant retrieved, and summaries with unsupported claims are flagged for review before the assistant is rolled out to fee-earners.

A hospital pharmacy team tests a clinical decision-support tool that retrieves guidelines and patient records. A clinician compares each generated treatment suggestion with the retrieved guideline text, and the team tracks the share of suggestions that go beyond what the sources say before the tool reaches ward staff.

A benefits agency tests its eligibility chatbot on questions drawn from real enquiries, including some the policy documents cannot answer. It checks that quoted amounts and rules match the retrieved policy text and that the chatbot says it cannot answer instead of guessing, before the chatbot is opened to citizens.

limitations.description: Scores that judge retrieval against known answers, such as context recall, need reference answers or labelled passages, which are slow to write and need experts in specialist domains. Reference-free scores avoid this but only penalise irrelevant passages, so they cannot show that a needed passage was never retrieved.

Scores usually come from a second language model acting as judge, so they inherit its errors and its sensitivity to wording. In the original Ragas study the judge agreed with human raters in 95% of pairwise comparisons on faithfulness but only 70% on context relevance, and it struggled to pick out the key sentences in long contexts.

Faithfulness measures whether an answer is supported by the retrieved text, not whether that text is correct, current or complete. A system that retrieves an outdated document and reports it accurately scores well, so the knowledge base needs checking separately.

Claim-by-claim checking may not catch answers that chain reasoning across several documents. Misleading emphasis, selective quotation and unsupported leaps between sources can pass when each sentence is individually supported, so these cases need targeted test questions and human review.

When a score is low, the cause can lie in retrieval, in generation or in how the two interact, and the scores alone often cannot say which. Diagnosis usually needs manual inspection of the retrieved passages and answers for a sample of failing questions.

resources.title: RAGAs: Automated Evaluation of Retrieval Augmented Generation
resources.abstract: We introduce RAGAs (Retrieval Augmented Generation Assessment), a framework for reference-free evaluation of Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) pipelines. RAGAs is available at [https://github.com/explodinggradients/ragas]. RAG systems are composed of a retrieval and an LLM based generation module. They provide LLMs with knowledge from a reference textual database, enabling them to act as a natural language layer between a user and textual databases, thus reducing the risk of hallucinations. Evaluating RAG architectures is challenging due to several dimensions to consider: the ability of the retrieval system to identify relevant and focused context passages, the ability of the LLM to exploit such passages faithfully, and the quality of the generation itself. With RAGAs, we introduce a suite of metrics that can evaluate these different dimensions without relying on ground truth human annotations. We posit that such a framework can contribute crucially to faster evaluation cycles of RAG architectures, which is especially important given the fast adoption of LLMs.

resources.title: Enhancing the Precision and Interpretability of Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) in Legal Technology: A Survey
resources.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is a promising solution that can enhance the capabilities of large language model (LLM) applications in critical domains, including legal technology, by retrieving knowledge from external databases. Implementing RAG pipelines requires careful attention to the techniques and methods implemented in the different stages of the RAG process. However, robust RAG can enhance LLM generation with faithfulness and few hallucinations in responses. In this paper, we discuss the application of RAG in the legal domain. First, we present an overview of the main RAG methods, stages, techniques, and applications in the legal domain. We then briefly discuss the different information retrieval models, processes, and applied methods in current legal RAG solutions. Then, we explain the different quantitative and qualitative evaluation metrics. We also describe several emerging datasets and benchmarks. We then discuss and assess the ethical and privacy considerations for legal RAG and summarize various challenges, and propose a challenge scale based on RAG failure points and control over external knowledge. Finally, we provide insights into promising future research to leverage RAG efficiently and effectively in the legal field.

resources.title: ASTRID - An Automated and Scalable TRIaD for the Evaluation of RAG-based Clinical Question Answering Systems
resources.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown impressive potential in clinical question answering (QA), with Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) emerging as a leading approach for ensuring the factual accuracy of model responses.However, current automated RAG metrics perform poorly in clinical and conversational use cases.Using clinical human evaluations of responses is expensive, unscalable, and not conducive to the continuous iterative development of RAG systems.To address these challenges, we introduce ASTRID -an Automated and Scalable TRIaD for evaluating clinical QA systems leveraging RAG -consisting of three metrics: Context Relevance (CR), Refusal Accuracy (RA), and Conversational Faithfulness (CF).Our novel evaluation metric, CF, is designed to better capture the faithfulness of a model's response to the knowledge base without penalizing conversational elements.Additionally, our metric RA captures the refusal to address questions outside of the system's scope of practice.To validate our triad, we curate a dataset of over 200 real-world patient questions posed to an LLM-based QA agent during surgical follow-up for cataract surgery -the highest volume operation in the worldaugmented with clinician-selected questions for emergency, and clinical and non-clinical out-of-domain scenarios.We demonstrate that CF predicts human ratings of faithfulness more accurately than existing definitions in conversational settings.Furthermore, using eight different LLMs, we demonstrate that the three metrics can closely agree with human evaluations, highlighting the potential of these metrics for use in LLM-driven automated evaluation pipelines.Finally, we show that evaluation using our triad of CF, RA, and CR exhibits alignment with clinician assessment for inappropriate, harmful, or unhelpful responses.We also publish the prompts and datasets for these experiments, providing valuable resources for further research and development.

techniques.name: Bootstrap Confidence Intervals for Evaluation Metrics
techniques.description: Bootstrap confidence intervals put a range around a model's measured performance, showing how much the score could differ had another test set of the same size been drawn from the same population. The labelled held-out evaluation set is resampled with replacement thousands of times, each resample holding as many cases as the original so that some cases appear more than once and others not at all, and the metric (an error rate, the area under a curve, a translation score) is recomputed on each resample from the model's stored predictions, with no retraining. The spread of these recomputed values stands in for the sampling distribution of the metric: the percentile interval takes its 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles for a 95 per cent interval, and the bias-corrected and accelerated (BCa) interval shifts those percentiles to correct for bias and skew in that distribution. The statistic can also be the difference between two models scored on the same cases, recomputed on each shared resample, which shows whether an observed improvement is larger than the noise from test-set sampling. The result is the metric with lower and upper bounds at a stated confidence level, so a requirement such as a maximum false-positive rate can be checked against the bound rather than the point estimate.

example_use_cases.description: A medical-imaging company preparing a regulatory submission reports its fracture detector's sensitivity and specificity at the locked threshold with 95 per cent bootstrap intervals. Because each patient contributes several radiographs, it resamples patients rather than images, so the interval reflects the number of independent patients in the test set rather than the larger number of images.

A machine-translation team deciding whether to replace its production model scores the current and candidate systems on the same held-out sentences, recomputes the difference in BLEU score on 1,000 shared bootstrap resamples of those sentences, and approves the change only if the 95 per cent interval for the difference lies above zero.

A fisheries agency whose vessel-detection model must keep false alarms below 2 per cent of non-vessel image patches re-measures the false-positive rate each quarter on several thousand newly labelled patches, puts a bootstrap interval on it, and states compliance against the interval's upper bound. In a quarter where the labelled sample yields only a handful of false positives, the agency uses an exact binomial interval instead, because the bootstrap interval is too narrow at that count.

An evaluation team comparing two large language models on a 500-question internal benchmark reports each model's accuracy with a BCa bootstrap interval and puts a paired interval on the difference, which shows that a 1.5-point lead is within the sampling noise of a test set that size, so the team does not cite it as evidence that one model is better.

limitations.description: For a rate built from rare errors, such as a low false-positive rate, the interval is too narrow when the test set holds only a handful of errors. With 200 negatives and a true rate of 0.5 per cent, about a third of test sets have no false positives; the percentile interval is then [0, 0] and BCa may return no value. For a single proportion the exact binomial (Clopper-Pearson) interval avoids this; the bootstrap earns its place on metrics with no simple formula.

Resampling single cases assumes they are independent. When several test cases come from one patient, vessel, user or time window, their errors are correlated, and resampling cases treats them as separate evidence, giving intervals that can be much too narrow. Resampling whole clusters (patients, days) instead restores the right width when there are enough clusters, which needs the cluster of each case to be recorded in the test set; with few clusters the interval is again too narrow.

The interval reflects only which cases happened to be in the test set. It says nothing about variation from retraining the model on other data or with another random seed, nor about whether the test set represents the deployment population, so a narrow interval on an unrepresentative test set is precise and still wrong. Uncertainty in a single prediction, from retraining on resampled training data, is a different procedure; see Bootstrap Ensembles.

If the decision threshold, the model or the metric was chosen by looking at the same test set, resampling that set leaves the interval centred on an optimistic estimate, because the selection effect is not reproduced in the resamples. The choice has to be made on data separate from the set that is resampled.

Coverage is approximate and improves with test-set size. Percentile intervals can be too narrow on small test sets, and more so for skewed metrics; the BCa interval corrects for bias and skew but not for the narrowness that comes from a small test set, so small test sets stay a problem. BCa also needs an extra leave-one-out pass over the test set, which is slow for large sets or costly metrics, and it returns no interval when every resample gives the same value.

resources.title: Bootstrap Methods: Another Look at the Jackknife
resources.abstract: We discuss the following problem: given a random sample X = (X1, X2, …, Xn) from an unknown probability distribution F, estimate the sampling distribution of some prespecified random variable R(X, F), on the basis of the observed data x. (Standard jackknife theory gives an approximate mean and variance in the case R(X, F) = θ(F̂) − θ(F), θ some parameter of interest.) A general method, called the "bootstrap," is introduced, and shown to work satisfactorily on a variety of estimation problems. The jackknife is shown to be a linear approximation method for the bootstrap. The exposition proceeds by a series of examples: variance of the sample median, error rates in a linear discriminant analysis, ratio estimation, estimating regression parameters, etc.

resources.title: Better Bootstrap Confidence Intervals
resources.abstract: We consider the problem of setting approximate confidence intervals for a single parameter θ in a multiparameter family. The standard approximate intervals based on maximum likelihood theory, , can be quite misleading. In practice, tricks based on transformations, bias corrections, and so forth, are often used to improve their accuracy. The bootstrap confidence intervals discussed in this article automatically incorporate such tricks without requiring the statistician to think them through for each new application, at the price of a considerable increase in computational effort. The new intervals incorporate an improvement over previously suggested methods, which results in second-order correctness in a wide variety of problems. In addition to parametric families, bootstrap intervals are also developed for nonparametric situations.
